title: New Zealand climbers rescued from Solomon Islands' highest mountain
text:
Two New Zealand men stranded on Solomon Islands' highest mountain have been rescued.

Keanu Isaksson, 25, and Luca Zylstra 19, were airlifted out of a steep ravine on Tuesday morning, where they had been trapped for the last six days.

Mr Isaksson's mother, Denise Holl, told the ABC a clear window of weather allowed a rescue helicopter to reach the pair, who were located 1,828 metres up Mount Popomanaseu in central Guadalcanal.

Mount Popomanaseu is a volcanic mountain on the Solomon Islands island of Guadalcanal. (Supplied)

It is understood the helicopter dropped food and a radio to the men, who were then able to clear space for a cargo net to be lowered.

"They instructed the boys to fell some trees to create some space for the helicopter," she said.

"The boys had their own equipment with knives that could do the tree work and they were able to climb the net and get flown back to Honiara."

Ms Holl said she was able to speak with the two men, describing them as both nonchalant and emotional.

"My son and Luca have done lots of adventures together and are very close, and they would have taken very good care of each other," she said.

Keanu Isaksson is an avid climber and has previously visited Mt Everest. (Supplied)

"I'm sure they've got quite a bit of footage and quite a few stories to tell."

Mr Isaksson and Mr Zylstra travelled to Solomon Islands in search of a remote climbing adventure and as preparation for an upcoming trip to the Amazon.

Mount Popomanaseu is a 2,335-metre mountain, taller than mainland Australia's tallest peak, Mount Kosciuszko, which stands at 2,228 metres.

Ms Holl said the friends had summitted with the aid of guides from a local tribe, but those guides could not take the men back down because the descent path crossed into a different tribal area.

During their descent, Ms Holl said torrential rain made the steep terrain "impossible" to traverse, forcing them to camp on a rock overlooking a waterfall for six days.

Reaching the summit of Mount Popomanaseu is a rugged multi-day expedition that requires local guides and custom clearances from local tribes. (Supplied: Visit Solomon Islands)

"They're extremely lucky that the rivers didn't rise any higher because it would have just washed them over the waterfall," she said.

Initial attempts to reach the pair were unsuccessful, with one search party forced to turn back because of heavy rain.

The rescue helicopter meanwhile did not have access to a winch and was unable to land where the men were stranded.

Ms Holl said the past week had taken a huge emotional toll on her family, but they could now rest easy knowing the men were safe.

"We're ecstatic, and I'm shaking right now and just decompressing," she said.

"We're just really happy that this didn't go on any longer."

title: Solo parenting wasn't for me, so I'm co-parenting with my sister
text:
As the hospital hummed with antiseptic quiet and Kathy's fingers gripped mine, I thought about how strange it was to be there at the very beginning of someone's life — a baby who was both mine and not mine.

But let's start back in 2019, when I was faced with a decision to have a baby of my own with one of my partners, and I decided not to.

I've always loved babies and kids — I had lots of younger cousins growing up, and my first job as a teenager was babysitting the kids down the road.

Yet having a kid of my own at the time didn't feel right for me. And that realisation sank me to the bottom of the sea.

Could I parent alone?

Fast-forward to 2021, and I was hyper focused on the prospect of solo parenting instead.

After careful consideration, Eli Sutherland realised solo parenting was not for them. (Supplied: Eli Sutherland)

I spent countless hours researching pregnancy and parenthood, intra-uterine insemination (IUI) and in vitro fertilisation (IVF), hospitals and home births, lactation cookies and swaddling techniques.

It was the perfect solution — everything on my own terms and timeline.

I spent $15,000 and submitted to a handful of painful tests, got the sperm delivered, and had the procedure. As soon as it went ahead, though, I knew it didn't feel right.

I didn't want to have biological children in that way, by myself, at that time. The procedure didn't take.

Solo parenting, it turns out, wasn't for me. But the process of discovering that also came with weekly phone calls with my sister, Kathy.

"I realised something," she said one day.

"It's funny how you're younger than me, but sometimes you lead me to realisations. I want to be a mum. I think I want to do IVF."

Do you have a unique co-parenting story to share with us? We'd love to hear from you.

Kathy came out as asexual and aromantic a few years ago and had maintained a stance of child-free-by-choice for years before that. Partly because babies meant a partner and sex (nope!) and partly because she's a primary school teacher, and that's enough kids to deal with on the daily.

Eli with their brother Andrew and sister Kathy. (Supplied: Eli Sutherland)

But accompanying me on my reproductive journey flicked a switch for Kathy — what became visible, became possible.

So we embarked on our own adventure

I'd been thinking about what it might mean to hold a child who isn't mine.

As a non-binary person, the label "maternal" fit me like a left shoe on a right foot, while "paternal" made me seasick.

Still, the pull was undeniable.

Kathy and I spent months planning what it would look like for me to move back to Perth/Boorloo from Melbourne/Naarm for the first six months of my nibling's life (for those who haven't heard of this term, nibling is a non-gendered combination of niece or nephew with sibling, i.e. a child of one's sibling).

Eli and their sister Kathy at the hospital. (Supplied: Eli Sutherland)

We also had some gentle (and sometimes less than gentle) conversations with people about our decision.

We explained, time and again, that:

"No, we're not a lesbian couple, we're siblings."

"I won't get paid parental leave, but I'm still taking six months off work to be the secondary co-parent."

"They'll have plenty of positive masculine role models, thanks."

"All this for a child that's not my own? Yes, I'm sure."

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

It was sometimes exhausting having to justify why our family looked different to others — a pregnant asexual woman, accompanied through birth and the newborn phase by a non-binary queer sibling.

But mostly it was wonderful to have conversations with people about what family means to them, and how that differs (and aligns) with what it means to us.

The moment that changed me

By August 2022, my sister and I were gowned in matching blue hospital attire, face masks and hairnets.

The gurney wheeled Kathy down the fluorescent-lit hallway towards the delivery room, her stomach stretched as far as it would go, holding a tiny human safe inside.

Eli with Kathy and their bub shortly after birth. (Supplied: Eli Sutherland)

And what a privilege it was to be in that delivery room. To be the first person to see, to hold, to kiss my nibling.

When she was finally placed on Kathy's chest, I felt something shift inside me.

Maybe that feeling is what parentalism means: a continual rebirth of the self, the family, the love we offer and lose.

Storm-grey seas revived to deepest blue.

In the years since, we've had four Christmases, dozens of trips to the beach, countless bubbles, and a whole lot of Bluey. Add to that the sleepless nights and bottle feeds, trips back and forth between cities, a few more IVF rounds, and now a baby brother heavyweight champion of chubby cheeks.

Eli and their nibling relaxing on the couch. (Supplied: Eli Sutherland)

Kathy will always be Mum to these two gorgeous kiddos, and I'll be something flowing in-between. Mostly I'm "Unty" (a gender-neutral mix of uncle and aunty), and sometimes just Eli.

But maybe the word isn't what's important.

Maybe what's important is just that I'll always be there with them.

Eli Sutherland (they/them) is an award-winning poet and writer living on Wurundjeri Country, and is the festival director of Trans Book Festival.

title: 'Cocaine dealer' on Mahmood Fazal's Four Corners episode says she did it as 'an acting role'
text:
Further concerns over the accuracy of reporting by sacked Four Corners reporter Mahmood Fazal have been raised on Media Watch, including that a hire car was used to mislead viewers in the profile of a purported cocaine dealer.

Fazal's employment was terminated after an ABC investigation into his appearance on a podcast with a former underworld figure last year, ABC managing director Hugh Marks confirmed at a Senate estimates hearing in May.

Since then, two episodes of Four Corners, Cocaine Nation and Meth Highway, have been removed by the ABC due to accuracy concerns.

On Friday, a Background Briefing audio program titled "Remy was 12 when she became a drug dealer" was also removed.

Loading...

In both the Background Briefing program and Cocaine Nation episode, Fazal interviewed Remy, a masked figure who is a purported cocaine dealer to Sydney's elite.

Now, Media Watch has reported that self-styled Sydney rapper Charissa Habkouk claims that she played the role of "Remy" as a favour to Fazal and that the core of her story in both programs was invented.

Ms Habkouk told Media Watch she considered Remy "an acting role and a favour to Mahmood".

"All of that … is a complete fable … there’s no validity to [it] … [Fazal] knew I could play the part and look the part," she told Media Watch.

Media Watch has alleged "Remy" was a role played by self-styled Sydney rapper Charissa Habkouk. (ABC: Four Corners)

She added that Fazal had approached her initially on Instagram, saying the story was "his shot to secure his work with the ABC".

In a response to Media Watch, Fazal rejected Ms Habkouk's claims and said he was "already contracted by the ABC on a permanent ongoing basis".

"The suggestion that I needed this story to 'cement' my position at the ABC is false," he said in a statement.

He added that he stood by the "integrity of my reporting and the editorial processes that underpinned both programs".

"I reject the suggestion that I fabricated, staged or knowingly published information that I believed to be false," Fazal said.

Mahmood Fazal was an investigative reporter for ABC RN's Background Briefing before his Four Corners role. (ABC)

Mercedes-Benz misleading in program

Media Watch reported Ms Habkouk alleged a Mercedes-Benz seen in the Four Corners episode was not hers, as the program implied, but hired by the ABC.

In the episode, a masked Ms Habkouk tells Fazal: "I’ve got us some nice wheels, a driver, take you to a few spots around Sydney."

She has since alleged the ABC "hired it, just to make it look like I was being driven around in it and there was an image".

Four Corners’ former executive producer Matthew Carney told Media Watch if Ms Habkouk's allegations "can be verified, then this is disappointing and troubling".

"If this information had been disclosed to me, the program would not have been broadcast," Carney said.

Ms Habkouk's claim cannot be immediately verified.

The ABC did not respond to Media Watch's questions.

Four Corners withdraws episodes The ABC has withdrawn the Four Corners programs Meth Highway and Cocaine Nation by sacked reporter Mahmood Fazal due to concerns about accuracy.

She also told Media Watch that her previous claims, made on social media, that she had been paid for the Four Corners appearance, were false, leading the program to say that her accounts of events should be treated with caution.

"I didn’t get paid for the role. Not by Mahmood or the ABC," she told the program.

The ABC has previously said Fazal's episodes were removed "following concerns identified about the veracity of sources used in the three programs".

"The ABC Ombudsman is already conducting an independent review of whether the Four Corners programs complied with the ABC's editorial standards," it added in a statement.

Fazal alleges reporting heavily scrutinised

Fazal, a former member of the Mongols bikie club, is an award-winning journalist specialising in crime, violence, imprisonment and terrorism.

ABC withdraws third story by Mahmood Fazal The ABC has withdrawn a third story by sacked reporter Mahmood Fazal due to concerns about accuracy.

Prior to joining the ABC, he worked for VICE as a senior staff writer and host of the series Violent Times.

His reporting has appeared in The Guardian, Rolling Stone, The Sydney Morning Herald, The Monthly and The Saturday Paper.

After the Four Corners episodes were removed, Fazal said in a statement posted to social media that he was “shocked” by the decision.

"I believe the process ABC is following and its decisions so far set a worrying precedent for the organisation's independent [sic] and commitment to public-interest journalism," he said.

In another lengthy video statement, Fazal claimed he was hired by the ABC for his access to certain sources, with that proximity later used to remove him from the organisation.

He said his reporting was heavily scrutinised during editorial standards and production meetings.

Charissa Habkouk says she played drug dealer Remy as a favour to Mahmood Fazal. (ABC: Four Corners)

"If there were questions about a source or a fact, we hashed it out internally at the time and made a call," Fazal said.

"And it wasn’t me making the call. Confidentiality doesn’t mean there was no oversight."

The withdrawals come at a turbulent time for the broadcaster after the sudden departure of news director Justin Stevens in May.

Mr Marks confirmed he and Stevens disagreed about the direction of the organisation and announced a replacement, Reuters executive editor Simon Robinson, the following day.

title: Aussie swimmer out of leadership group after reported drinking session
text:
Australian swimmer Isaac Cooper has stepped down from the Dolphins's leadership group after a drinking session at the Commonwealth Games.

Cooper was reported to be out drinking when he was expected to be supporting teammates at Glasgow's Tollcross International Swimming Centre last Wednesday night.

Cooper was also seen drinking at the Australian team hotel during that day, the report said.

"Isaac did not attend the final night of the swimming competition or final team meeting in Glasgow, which is in conflict with team expectations," a Swimming Australia statement said.

What the Commonwealth Games mean is up to you Australian chef de mission and eight-time Olympic medallist Petria Thomas cried as she spoke about the importance of the Commonwealth Games to her, so it doesn't really matter if it felt too easy for Australia at times.

"Isaac has since voluntarily stood down from the team's athlete leadership group."

Cooper was scheduled to race the 100m backstroke final that night but withdrew from the event after qualifying eighth-fastest.

Swimmers were expected to support teammates at the Glasgow Games when not racing, while Cooper also missed the team meeting that night.

The 22-year-old won gold at the Glasgow Games as a member of the 4x100m medley team after swimming in the heats.

He also finished sixth in the 50m backstroke final, an event he won a silver medal at the 2024 world championships.

Cooper will next compete at the Pan Pacific championships in the United States starting August 12.

AAP

title: Death toll from Venezuela earthquakes tops 6,000
text:
The death toll from twin ‌earthquakes which struck Venezuela in June has risen to 6,125, according to figures released by top lawmaker Jorge Rodríguez.

Mr Rodríguez, head of Venezuela's National Assembly, posted details on Telegram showing nearly 61,000 people were treated in hospitals.

He said 16.5 per cent of the debris generated by the quakes had been removed.

The 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude quakes struck on June 24, hitting within 39 seconds of each other and causing nearly 200 buildings to collapse, mostly in the worst-hit coastal state of La Guaira.

The quakes caused nearly 200 buildings to collapse. (Reuters: Gaby Oraa)

Last month the World Bank estimated the quakes caused $US19.6 billion ($28 billion) in direct physical damage, but the cost of rebuilding could be twice that much ‌or more.

Acting President Delcy Rodríguez, who US President Donald Trump backs, has defended the government's response amid criticism that military personnel and other officials arrived late and have done little to help victims of the quake, including people who were trapped in the rubble.

About 1,400 still missing

Rescue teams and family members continue to sift through the rubble in search of victims and loved ones.

Local media quoted La Guaira Governor Jose Alejandro Teran as saying about 1,400 people remain missing after the disaster.

Thousands of volunteers and humanitarian workers have joined relief efforts. (AP: Matias Delacroix, File)

The government has not otherwise disclosed how many people are missing, but expert projections have put the figure at up to 10,000.

In addition to the 190 buildings that were destroyed, authorities have classified over 16,200 structures as unsafe, prompting many to leave.

Almost 24,000 people in La Guaira and Caracas are living in makeshift shelters following the earthquakes.

People affected by the earthquakes line up for food in La Guaira. (P: Matias Delacroix, File)

Venezuelan lawmakers approve rental bill

Venezuelan lawmakers last week unanimously approved a law that makes it easier to rent properties.

The measure, which aims to help displaced quake victims, repeals anti-rental legislation passed by former leftist Chavista administrations.

"We are estimating around 400,000 homes that could benefit from this law," interim leader Delcy Rodríguez said Monday, local time, describing a "win-win" situation for tenants and property owners.

Ms Rodríguez previously pledged to provide 4,000 homes to quake victims by the end of the year, with the government aiming for that number to exceed 10,000 in 2027.

Reuters/AFP

title: Councils push to set their own rates for mining companies
text:
The Local Government Association of the Northern Territory (LGANT) is seeking legislative changes to allow councils to determine mining rates within their own areas, in a bid to increase their financial sustainability.

Currently under the Local Government Act 2019, the NT minister for local government sets the rates for mining tenements and pastoral leases, instead of allowing councils to set the rates, as they do for other properties.

But LGANT president Peter Pangquee said councils should be able to rate mining companies the same as they did other ratepayers, based on the size of their properties.

"We appreciate the mining industry and what they do for the Northern Territory, but what we want is a bit of fairness," he said.

Local Government Association of the Northern Territory (LGANT) president Peter Pangquee. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Mr Pangquee said most councils in the NT had small populations and few rateable properties, meaning a smaller revenue base, which made it hard for councils to upgrade infrastructure and provide services.

"Currently the mining industry pays $1.6 million right across the Territory to all councils," he said.

"That's not a lot when you look at the proportion of intake by those companies."

Council's costs soaring

A report by the Industry Capability Network NT showed mining across the NT was set to boom, with the operations in the Barkly region alone expected to generate $35 billion by 2030.

Barkly Regional Council Mayor Sid Vashist said only a small amount of that money was flowing back to the council, yet the council was struggling to maintain its roads, fleet vehicles and infrastructure.

Sid Vashist is the mayor of the Barkly Regional Council. (ABC News: Will Green)

"Under the conditional rating system in the Northern Territory, it's not great for the councils," he said.

"A mine in Queensland that's producing gold is potentially paying between $130,000 to $250,000 in rates to a council. Currently, we might have mines in our region that will be potentially paying between $10,000 to $15,000, so the disparity is huge."

The Tennant Creek library's broken windows are boarded up, adding to the costs. (ABC Alice Springs: Victoria Ellis)

Mr Vashist said it would cost council $155 million over 10 years to maintain its assets, but council would only have a spare $5 million to use over the same amount of time.

Meanwhile, he said damage to council buildings from vandalism and antisocial behaviour could cost millions of dollars to fix.

"I'm not proud about it and we need to change that story, but we don't have the cash to do it," he said.

Industry rejects rate rises

Minerals Council of Australia executive director of Northern Australia Cathryn Tilmouth said increasing rate payments would disincentivise the mining industry from operating in the Northern Territory, where it made a huge economic contribution.

"It's not just about the rates that are paid, you've got employment, you've got service and supply industry getting contracts from these projects, you've got all the infrastructure that mining projects actually deliver that the government couldn't otherwise," she said.

Cathryn Tilmouth says mining contributes a lot to the NT economy. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

Ms Tilmouth said rates were meant to be paid in return for service provision, but councils were not providing services to mines.

"What is the mining industry actually getting from local government? Rubbish collection, streetlights, roadworks, they're not getting any of that," she said.

"The mining industry is fairly self-sustainable in that area."

The Minister for Local Government Steve Edgington said he would make "evidence-based decisions", but he had to "balance" all the things that came with mining development against the benefits.

title: Billion-dollar property collapse highlights private credit danger
text:
Jon Adgemis raised the white flag last October.

With forces closing in from all sides, he declared himself bankrupt to avoid the ignominy of being compelled by his long list of creditors into a life of penury.

His hospitality dream in ruins, the former Maserati-loving playboy somehow managed to rack up $1.8 billion in debt — much of it from private credit firms — over a hotel portfolio that cost less than $300 million to assemble.

Liquidators will attempt to unravel the mystery behind Adgemis's incredible rise and spectacular fall later this week when they begin examinations in the Federal Court.

A conga line of former business associates and love interests have been requested to produce records of their dealings with the one-time KPMG high-flyer.

But there are broader implications.

The examinations of the Adgemis property downfall may well shed light on the extent to which private credit firms, essentially a shadow banking industry with little or no regulation, have their hooks into the economy.

Born out of the tighter regulatory climate after the global financial crisis, they blossomed in Australia in the wake of the Hayne royal commission into banking misconduct.

The Adgemis hearings come at a crucial inflexion point.

ASIC raises alarm on private credit ASIC is concerned about the risks posed by private credit for Australians with superannuation.

The Australian property market appears to be on the cusp of a prolonged downturn, the first since 2017.

That is likely to plunge property developers, the group that overwhelmingly relies upon non-bank loans, into a world of pain that could ripple through to builders and subcontractors.

And it follows warnings from Australia's corporate regulator, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC), about the dangers building within this largely unregulated arena.

ASIC commissioner Simone Constant is concerned about the potential for a private credit financial shock. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Marketed with limited regulatory oversight, the industry has attracted cash from retirees and investors seeking high returns in what many mistakenly believe are safe mortgages.

From tiny amounts just a decade ago, ASIC estimates that close to $250 billion in loans are outstanding, an amount that could inflict serious pain on the economy if large numbers of these loans soured.

When friends fall out

Jon Adgemis was the consummate networker.

A deal maker who cultivated an image of success, he advised some of the nation's biggest firms and befriended billionaires in his quest for success.

WIN TV owner Bruce Gordon was once a fan. So too was Jan Cameron, the force behind Kathmandu. Both severed ties with him after disputes over money six years ago.

He bought his first pub in 2015 in Balmain, Sydney, adding another three in the trendy inner west over the next two years.

But from 2020 on, right through the COVID-19 lockdowns, he added another 14 establishments, mostly in Sydney with a few in Melbourne.

Jon Adgemis amassed a property portfolio under Public Hospitality Group. (Instagram: commercial.ready)

Many needed extensive renovations, and, while work was started on some, few were ever completed, and some stood idle.

It is expected the liquidators will examine how Adgemis was able to continue raising cash, given the limited earnings the properties generated.

One avenue of inquiry will centre on whether the property valuations, many of which were increased shortly after purchase, were reasonable.

Property killed productivity With housing prices coming off the boil, maybe our banks will start lending to more productive areas of the economy, like business.

Investors who tipped money into the acquisitions generally had little idea where their cash was being deployed.

In most cases, they had invested in a private credit fund that had promised double-digit returns on properties with claims they were protected by strong mortgage backing.

In some cases, the credit funds were charging upwards of 20 per cent interest on loans to developers, indicating the loans were high-risk.

Many developers have difficulty getting loans from traditional sources given the huge outlays required for construction and the long lag times before sales begin to generate revenues.

By the time his Public Hospitality Group collapsed, many of the properties had multiple mortgages.

The private debt trap

The red lights have been flashing for more than a year.

Operating outside the banking system and largely unregulated, private credit is an industry that has many worried, particularly if there is a severe stock market correction or economic downturn.

ASIC has been concerned for some time about the incredible growth in private credit, not just local funds but international funds seeking cash from Australians.

A fortnight ago it issued warnings, advising funds to ensure their valuations were "current, accurate and grounded in realistic assumptions".

"The sector is facing its first real test," it warned.

" Tighter liquidity, emerging borrower stress and signs of credit deterioration are testing valuations, governance and investor disclosures. "

Have interest rates already peaked? With two Australian banks cutting fixed home loan rates, there is a ray of hope that the cycle of interest rate hikes has peaked and borrowing costs may be lower down the track — another sign the pace of economic change has moved into overdrive.

The Reserve Bank of Australia is also concerned.

A sustained property downturn could impact the financial sector while the rupture of a major global fund could also have spillover effects here.

Globally, private credit is huge.

In the US, the Financial Stability Board estimates the market has ballooned to be worth upwards of $US2 trillion ($2.85 trillion), a system that essentially flies under the radar.

"In the past, private credit mostly focused on medium-sized businesses and was available only to institutional investors, such as pension funds and insurance companies," it notes.

More recently, it has been accessed by mega technology companies in their quest to finance their high-risk ambitions in the race for artificial intelligence superiority.

What could go wrong?

"Private credit at its current size and scope has not been tested during a severe economic downturn, which could expose leverage and borrower credit quality vulnerabilities," it notes.

High returns, high risk

This isn't the first time property developers have been caught in a credit vice that has then flowed through to investors.

As the global financial crisis hit in 2007, a wave of property developers that had been raising cash from retail investors at interest rates substantially higher than term deposits all hit the wall.

Loading

Bridgecorp, Fincorp, Westpoint and Banksia Securities were raising cash via what's known as debentures with investors mistakenly believing they had first mortgage protection over the properties to which they were lending.

This time around, investors may be even less well-informed about the ultimate destination of their funds.

Ratings Agency SQM Research recently downgraded a local private credit fund run by investors Centuria Capital.

It downgraded the Centuria Bass Credit Fund, which has $300 million in investments, describing it as uninvestable because of lending to a Sydney apartment developer, Bathla.

Loading...

SQM has previously highlighted problems with transparency in the sector.

Aggressive marketing and a lack of clarity about the borrowers' exact identity were high on the list of concerns.

(Worth noting SQM Research is under its own scrutiny, with ASIC suing it over its ratings of the Shield Master Fund before its collapse.)

As the real estate downturn gathers pace, the pressure on developers will only increase.

Loading...

According to property monitoring firm Cotality, price falls are accelerating in the two big markets of Sydney and Melbourne and widening to include Brisbane, Adelaide and Canberra, while gains in the remaining capitals are slowing.

That puts a squeeze on developer profit margins, making it tougher to continue funding half-finished projects.

Those losses would then begin to back up into self-managed super funds and private investors who have jumped aboard the private credit express.

In the meantime, many are eagerly awaiting the public hearings for Public Hospitality, and are keen to hear from Adgemis personally when he takes the stand in the liquidator's hearing.

title: Injured SA greyhound trainer ordered to return $40k in compensation
text:
A greyhound trainer who was struck by a 28-kilogram "mechanical lure" has been ordered to return $40,000 in compensation to South Australia's peak racing body.

The SA Employment Tribunal awarded the sum to the trainer last year after Safework SA secured a criminal conviction against Greyhound Racing SA [GRSA].

But GRSA has appealed the decision, with the same tribunal now finding the compensation had been given without proper processes being followed under the Sentencing Act.

The tribunal has also found GRSA's fine should be reduced from $255,000 to $180,000, as the organisation should have received the maximum benefit for entering an early guilty plea.

No compensation case submitted

The tribunal said the fine and compensation relate to injuries sustained by a trainer who used an unauthorised shortcut to exit a racing start area in September 2022.

This put him "in close proximity to the mechanical lure whilst trials were occurring", causing him to be struck while it travelled at around 70 kilometres per hour.

Greyhounds chasing a mechanical lure at the Angle Park race track. (Supplied: Greyhound Racing SA)

The incident left him with "fractures, broken teeth and mouth lacerations which required hospitalisation and two lots of surgery", according to the court decision handed down last week.



The tribunal found GRSA liable for the injuries in 2025 as it "had not undertaken an adequate risk assessment".

Despite this, on appeal, the tribunal said neither the trainer nor Safework SA formally submitted a case for compensation in the original court proceedings.

This is a requirement under the Sentencing Act

"There was no evidence before the court in relation to the quantum of [the trainer's] loss and expense," the judgement from last week said.

"No representations were made on the issue of compensation.

"In the absence of those things, the court did not have a proper basis on which to award compensation."

The tribunal found Greyhound Racing SA "had not undertaken an adequate risk assessment". (ABC News)

Fine total slashed

In November 2025, the tribunal handed down a $300,000 fine to be paid to Safework SA.

It originally ruled a 15 per cent discount was "all that could be justified" as GRSA had refused to voluntarily compensate the trainer and offer a direct apology.

It left the organisation with a $255,000 penalty.

On appeal, the tribunal found GRSA's "failure to contact [the victim]" was based on legal advice around a separate damages claim the victim was pursuing.

It reduced the fine total to $180,000 and ordered Safework SA to pay GRSA's legal fees but upheld the criminal conviction against the racing body.

GRSA declined to comment further on the court's decision.

title: WA's Mid West faces hurdles to hosting Australia's newest oil refinery
text:
Power constraints remain one of the Oakajee industrial site's biggest hurdles as the Commonwealth explores locations for a potential new oil refinery in Western Australia, according to a regional chamber of commerce leader.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and WA Premier Roger Cook last week announced a $4 million pre-feasibility study to examine potential sites.

With the announcement being made in the state's mining hub of Karratha, there was some confusion about which areas were being explored for the refinery.

But WA Energy Minister Amber Jade Sanderson said the Mid West and South West were the main locations of interest.

The Oakajee Industrial Area was developed to create a new heavy industrial area. (ABC News: Chris Lewis)

Power investment needed

Ms Sanderson said a refinery in WA "just makes sense" and many ideal locations had already been identified.

"The feasibility study will examine all location options across WA including Oakajee, Kwinana or Kemerton," she said.

The Oakajee Strategic Industrial Area, 440 kilometres north of Perth, was designed to create a heavy industrial hub.

The site, which covers 1,330 hectares of land, sits adjacent to the ocean.

It was identified more than 20 years ago for a potential second port, but nothing has been developed

Mid West Chamber of Commerce chief executive Joanne Fabling said a lack of power supply to the region was a major hurdle to attracting new businesses.

Joanne Fabling says a lack of power infrastructure in Geraldton is stopping industry from developing further. ( ABC News: Phoebe Pin )

The state government announced in 2025 it would expand the high-capacity Clean Energy Link North from Malaga to Three Springs but not the 140 kilometres further to connect Geraldton, WA's second-largest regional city.

Ms Fabling said infrastructure was deterring potential business investment and a 330KV transmission line was needed to connect the whole region.

"We have long known that the Mid West has power constraints, especially even for our existing businesses and supply," she said.

" It's hurting our opportunities to progress major projects … that would deliver great return on investment. "

Transmission lines run from Malaga to Three Springs. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

Legislation prevents private entities from controlling public property, such as power infrastructure, which Ms Fabling said created red tape around further development.

"So if someone has to go and build a 330KV transmission line from Three Springs to Oakajee, they wouldn't be able to own it if it was connecting back into the grid," she said.

"No-one [wants] to make the first move on a particular project that's probably sitting around $300 odd million to do."

Ms Fabling said she was not holding her breath when the government announced it would explore Oakajee as a site for a new oil refinery.

"One of the things that we really know is there's a lot of water between an announcement and anything progressing," she said.

A new road at the Oakajee site leads to empty land. (ABC News: Chris Lewis)

Analyst at the Institute for Energy, Economics and Financial Analysis, Kevin Morrison, said the Mid West's power issues would have to be addressed if the refinery came to Oakajee.

"Petrol refineries do require a lot of energy, not just electricity but also gas, largely because the crude oil has to be heated and broken down," he said.

"So that would be an additional investment for a new refinery if it's going to be located in the Mid West."

'Still dependent' on imports

Experts have started poking holes in the plan since the announcement for a study was made.

Mr Morrison said if the project got off the ground, it most likely would not change the country's reliance on imported oil.

Kevin Morrison says power issues would need to be addressed. (ABC News: James Carmody)

"Geoscience Australia have assessed the commercial oil reserves; that is what makes economic sense to extract out of the ground [which] equates to only about seven months of daily consumption," he said.

"[With a WA refinery] We are still going to be dependent on importing oil, but we'll just be importing crude oil instead of oil products.

"I just think there needs to be an emphasis; it's really not going to change our energy security situation."

title: Blues announce King as new Origin coach after Daley steps down
text:
Former NSW State of Origin player Matt King has been named the new head coach of the Blues.

King was announced as the new coach on Tuesday after predecessor Laurie Daley stepped down from the role on Monday.

Blues pay tribute to 'hero' Daley as he stands down as coach The NSWRL pays tribute to Blues "hero" Laurie Daley as the coach stands down from his role after this year's series win over Queensland.

King played nine times for the Blues from 2005-2007, and over 200 first grade matches for Melbourne, South Sydney and Warrington across the NRL and Super League in England.

"I'm very clear on what it looks like to be the head coach of NSW," King said.

"I have a true understanding of what it means to lead this great state of ours and I can't wait for that opportunity.

"The one true rugby league love of my life has been the NSW Blues. To know now that I have the opportunity to guide the team moving forward, to lead the program over the next little period, means the absolute world to me."

The 45-year-old has been a long-time assistant coach under Trent Robinson at the Sydney Roosters, and has been part of the Blues' coaching staff since 2024.

Daley stepped down as Blues coach on Monday after guiding NSW to a series win this year.

The Blues sealed the series with a 30-12 triumph in the decider at Lang Park, just the fourth time NSW has won a deciding Game III in Brisbane.

Daley slams 'hidden agendas' after NSW Origin win Laurie Daley has the last laugh over critics who hounded him ahead of the State of Origin decider at Lang Park.

"I've always considered it an absolute honour and privilege to be involved with the NSW Blues State of Origin team, whether that was as a player or a coach, and I've always been ready to answer the call for my state whenever they needed me," Daley said in a statement on Monday.

"We faced plenty of challenges in the 2026 series and I'm proud of the way the players banded together to overcome them and save their best performance for Game Three in Brisbane to secure a memorable series win.

"I thank the fans for their passion and their support, and I can't think of a better way to move on with the Shield back where it belongs in NSW."

title: 'Nature doesn't follow your plans': Solo walker recounts rescue from Overland Track
text:
An "overly prepared" Tasmanian adventurer has recounted her rescue by helicopter from the Overland Track after the weather turned and she fell into an icy river.

Fiona Weaver runs an adventure tourism business with her husband in southern Tasmania and has spent decades exploring the state's great outdoors.

She found herself relying on that experience while on the 65-kilometre Overland Track last week.

Ms Weaver told 936 ABC Hobart that, initially, she had planned to do the four-day walk with a friend, but her friend had to pull out at the last minute.

Ms Weaver said that, after discussing it, she decided to proceed with the trip alone, carrying an emergency locator beacon and six days' worth of supplies and knowing she was set to meet a different friend part-way through.

Ditching law to take women into the wilderness After working in law in Sydney, Fiona Weaver gave it all up to start a nature tourism business which encourages Tasmanian women to become 'wild'.

"I knew my risk, I had a friend, I had someone meeting me at the end, I had a shuttle bus, I spoke to the rangers in charge," Ms Weaver said.

"I would say I was overly prepared, if that is even a word, for having a hike in the woods."

Travelling south to north, the first part of the trip went smoothly.

However, late on day two there was an unexpected heavy downpour, which had her reassessing the journey.

When the weather cleared the following morning, she decided to continue on, encountering what she described as "extensive" park maintenance while travelling through the Forth River Valley.

It was during this leg of the trip, later in the day, that she fell off a wooden crossing, falling into an icy river and becoming separated from her hiking bag.

"I was submerged into about 45 centimetres of water," Ms Weaver said.

Ms Weaver said that, fortunately, she had a torch on her wrist and so she gave herself 10 minutes to relocate her pack.

After assessing if she was injured, she decided to return to New Pelion Hut, where she had come from, "cold, soaked and exhausted".

Fiona Weaver says she was "cold, soaked and exhausted" when she decided to return to New Pelion Hut. (Wikimedia: Ash Sydney)

Going hiking? You should take a locator beacon — here's how to use it When you go hiking, experts say a personal locator beacon should be a non-negotiable. So how do they work, and where do you get one?

The hut, she said, had no lighting and the heater was out of action.

There, she decided to activate her emergency beacon, getting into spare clothes and an emergency blanket which had been protected in her dry bag.

However, Ms Weaver said, as the EPIRB had been submerged, she was not sure if the message had gone through.

"About 12 hours later, warming up in the sun and preparing to head back to Kia Ora [Hut] to dry out… I heard the unmistakable roar of the Westpac Rescue Helicopter", she said, in a post about her hike on social media.

"I cannot put into words the gratitude I feel for the crew who brought me safely home," she said.

Tasmania Police confirmed it was notified a woman "had activated her personal locator beacon about 2:30am Wednesday, 29 July".

"Tasmania Police Search and Rescue teams, including the Westpac Rescue Helicopter, located the woman shortly after 11am … at the Pelion Hut."

Hikers on the Overland must be flexible and have contingency plans, police say. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

'Nature doesn't always follow your plans'

Ms Weaver said she did not want to discourage anyone, particularly women, from exploring the outdoors.

Think you can handle the Overland Track? Tasmania's wild places continue to captivate travellers, but experts say it is easy to underestimate how quickly a sunny day can flip to life-threatening conditions. One SES rescuer shares his advice for staying safe in the wilderness.

"I'm sharing this story not to discourage anyone from exploring these remarkable places, but to remind us all that nature doesn't always follow your plans," she said.

"Sometimes, no matter how well you prepare, the wilderness reminds you who's really in charge."

She said it was important to be well prepared, but also to recognise that "no amount of experience or planning makes us immune to the unexpected".

Multiple rescues carried out

Influencers and winter hiking Don't plan a bushwalk based on what an Instagram influencer may have supposedly achieved, a veteran rescuer says, ahead of Tasmania's winter season.

Ms Weaver is one of several hikers who have been assisted in Tasmania's wilderness in recent weeks, with four people rescued in three separate incidents at the weekend.

Tasmania Police said bushwalkers were urged to be prepared for trips, and to always carry appropriate safety equipment.

They said this included carrying sufficient warm clothing, food and emergency communication devices, and that they "strongly advised against" walking alone.

"Be mindful that assistance may take some time to arrive depending on the location and weather. You must be prepared to survive until assistance arrives," Tasmania Police said.

"Be flexible and have a contingency plan.

"Be prepared to turn back or change plans if severe weather is forecast or eventuates during the walk, or the trip is harder than you thought.

title: Top End's first potato crop in decades almost ready for harvest
text:
One of Australia's biggest potato suppliers is just days away from harvesting its first crop in the Northern Territory, which has not been grown in the region for decades.

Zerella Holdings has grown about 70 hectares of seed potatoes at its farm just north of Katherine.

From next week, the Territory-grown tubers will be freighted by rail to the company's farms in the Northern Adelaide plains, where they will sprout into food-grade potatoes early next year.

Jake Pye has moved to the Katherine region to manage the seed potato farm, which is owned and operated by his South Australian relatives. (ABC News: Sam Parry)

In May, the company planted its first pivot-irrigated crop of low-carbohydrate Maranca variety at its newly established farm.

The eight-week harvest will employ a mixture of backpackers and local workers.

Once complete, it would mark the first successful commercial potato production in the Top End for about 20 years.

A crop of seed potatoes grown at Eagle Park, near Katherine, NT. (ABC News: Sam Parry)

Farm manager Jacob Pye said the conditions had been excellent for Zerella's operation.

"It's a nice, fast, growing season with a good mix of soils for growing potatoes," Mr Pye said.

Mr Pye said the Top End's warm weather conditions allowed for a much shorter growing season than at Zerella's other sites.

"It's not causing too much stress on the potatoes at all, and the water up here has been magnificent," Mr Pye said.



He said a shorter production window meant the work could be completed before the wet season.

During the harvest, seed potatoes will be processed and stored in a newly constructed facility on the site at Florina, NT. (ABC News: Sam Parry)

A processing plant and cool room facility is also being built on the site.

Previous potato growers in the Top End had successfully grown a crop, but high input costs and competition from established operations interstate had prevented commercial viability in the Northern Territory.

Seed potatoes grown at the farm will be loaded into 1-tonne bags before being sent south in refrigerated rail containers. (ABC News: Sam Parry)

Pigs pose challenge

Mr Pye said feral pigs had damaged a portion of the crop but the company was confident it could manage the impact of the pests, and they would not be a threat to production.

"Being from New Zealand, I've never really heard of pigs getting into your potatoes, so that was a bit of a bit of an eye-opener for me, personally," he said.

"They sort of just root up the ground a bit, looking for that moisture, that's all they sort of want.

The company is confident it can manage the impact of feral pigs. (Supplied: Neil Edwards )

"It's not like they're wiping out a whole pivot or anything — they have a little bit of a nibble on the end, maybe, but that would be about it."

Mr Pye said a significant wet season, which saw the town of Katherine inundated by floodwaters, had also been successfully navigated.

title: Melbourne public hospital doctors to strike next week
text:
Victorian doctors will walk off the job next week at some of the state's busiest hospitals as part of a pay dispute with the state government.

It will be the first protected industrial action at Victorian public hospitals for 20 years.

The Australian Medical Association Victoria (AMAV) said public hospital doctors will stop work at hospitals in Parkville and Melbourne's CBD for several hours on August 13.

The work ban, involving members of the Australian Salaried Medical Officers Federation, will run from 12:30pm until 4pm and workers will rally in Grattan Street in the city.

Hospitals affected include the Royal Melbourne Hospital, the Royal Children's Hospital and the Royal Women's Hospital as well as other facilities.

AMAV said affected hospitals have been asked to reschedule non-life-threatening appointments on that day.

The Victorian branch of the Australian Salaried Medical Officers Federation is set to take industrial action ahead of the November state election. (Unsplash: Frederick Medina)

It is understood doctors in emergency departments and other critical frontline services will not take part in the work ban.

AMAV president Simon Judkins said doctors had tried to negotiate a better deal with the government over pay and conditions for 12 months.

"Up to 50 per cent of, particularly our doctors in training, report incredibly high levels of fatigue and stress, and they're incredibly worried in those conditions about whether they might be prone to making errors," he said.

"Many of our doctors still don't get paid for overtime, a lot of our consultants are on call after hours and don't get paid for overtime.

"We're also looking at shifts, shift fatigue, making sure doctors get adequate breaks when they're on work."

AMAV said 97 per cent of union members voted in favour of the protected industrial action.

In addition to the work bans at the major Melbourne public hospitals, doctors will also begin other statewide actions, such as disrupting billing of patients and refusing to do unscheduled overtime.

Doctors will also refuse to answer emails and phone calls from hospital management.

title: With a new heart, 18-month-old Noah is finally coming home
text:
After enduring the unimaginable, the Forster family are set for an emotional cross-country journey home to Western Australia.

Their 18-month-old son Noah has had a successful heart transplant, surviving the condition that claimed the life of his older brother Teddy.

Little Noah is ready to come home to Busselton in WA after a successful heart transplant. (Supplied: Sinead Forster)

Sinead and Alex Forster's second son was just six days old when he was diagnosed with ventricular non-compaction dilated cardiomyopathy, affecting his heart's left ventricle.

Teddy, the couple's firstborn son, died waiting for a transplant at 20 months old.

"We didn't want the fear of what had happened to Teddy to stop us from trying again," Ms Forster said.

Ms Forster said the young family moved to Melbourne for medical care soon after Noah was diagnosed.

It was a decision that saved his life, his mother said.

"They wanted to get Noah in a place that could give him the best possible support before he got very, very sick," Ms Forster said.

Noah Forster will make a road trip home, with the family opting to drive as his immune system recovers. (Supplied: Sinead Forster)

Call 'we never thought would come'

Noah went into heart failure at seven months old, and was kept alive by a ventricular assist device.

After nine long months, the family received the call that a suitable donor had been found.

"You're waiting for this phone call that you never thought will come," Ms Forster said.

" To receive that call and to be told that your child has a chance at a life, and you can move on from this limbo that you've been living in, takes your breath away. "

Joy after tragedy

For the Forsters, the memory of their first son Teddy is ever present.

"[Noah has] always got his big brother Teddy watching over him so he can accomplish anything," Ms Forster said.

Noah was their "rainbow baby", their chance for a family after the devastating loss of Teddy, she explained.

The Forsters tragically lost their first-born, Teddy, to heart complications. (Supplied: Sinead Forster)

Ms Forster said cardiologists had told the couple they had a one-in-two chance of having another child with a similar condition.

"We thought, let's take the chance, let's try and have a family," she said.

"Being pregnant with another child and not knowing the future was very scary.

"After such a long time of waiting and then still losing Teddy, this baby was going to be our second chance."

Teddy died while waiting for a donor heart. (Supplied: Sinead Forster)

The Forsters are also painfully aware, as they celebrated the life of their second son, that the family of their donor was grieving.

"We will forever be thankful for that family, and for that child for this amazing gift that they've given our son," she said.

" They've really given him a chance at life. Not even a second chance. This is a chance at life. "

Family's courage praised

Heart Kids regional family support coordinator Ariana Potts met the Forsters after the birth of their first son Teddy.

"They are the most compassionate and generous family, and they have shown immense courage," she said.

Ms Potts said the experience could be incredibly isolating, and creating a support network is very important.

"It's an incredibly difficult time for all the families, and I think they need as much support as possible," Ms Potts said.

Organ donor opt-out A proposal to automatically make people organ donors could reduce the number of available organs.

Long trip home

Noah, now recovering from the surgery, is ready to return home.

The family is choosing to drive, in a bid to protect his vulnerable immune system.

The drive is also a chance for the family to make lasting memories.

"Putting an 18-month-old on a plane, where we can't get him to wear a mask, we can't protect him from the germs around us," Ms Forster said.

"This will be our last chance together before normal life begins."

Noah had shown resilience, with a smile on his face, throughout the ordeal.

title: How a father's love of music took his daughter to the world stage
text:
How do you raise a musical child?

What if she becomes more famous than you?

For baritone Christopher Allan and his daughter, soprano Miriam Allan, a love of music matters more than success or fame.

Christopher Allan raised his family in Newcastle, NSW. When Miriam grew up, her career took her to the UK, where she is now raising her own family in the town of Windsor.

At the height of the COVID-19 lockdowns, Miriam Allan attracted international attention as the soprano in the four-person choir that accompanied Prince Philip's scaled-back funeral at St George's Chapel, Windsor.

Her father watched proudly from his home in Newcastle.

Despite living on opposite sides of the world, Christopher and Miriam Allan share a close bond built on their love of music and music education.

Miriam and Christopher Allan last appeared onstage together in Newcastle in 2019. (Supplied: Photolook Newcastle)

Now, they're preparing to tour JS Bach's Coffee Cantata, showing the composer's lighter side through the story of a father trying (and failing) to stop his daughter from drinking too much coffee.

We talk with Christopher and Miriam Allan about their family's love of music, navigating life across continents, and why each considers the other their favourite performing partner.

On raising a musical child …

Christopher: Music was always around.

I've got photos of Mim [Miriam] in her bassinet underneath the harpsichord while we were rehearsing.

She started piano lessons at five, and we soon realised she has perfect pitch.

She joined the cathedral choir in Newcastle when she turned six.

By the time she was 18, she'd already sung on the ABC, and done some professional gigs with the Song Company.

I was teaching at Newcastle Conservatorium when Miriam decided to study music.

We had to arrange for her to be taught by a teacher from another university.

Otherwise, it would've been impossible to assess her.

On having a musical parent …

Miriam: I have so many memories of sitting down at the piano and playing with Dad when I was a little kid.

Miriam Allan has fond memories of her dad, Christopher Allan, playing the piano when she was growing up. (ABC Newcastle: Sofie Wainwright)

I remember seeing Dad sing on major stages, including the Sydney Opera House, when I was a teenager.

And Dad was involved in a huge number of education projects where he would get kids singing in any way, shape or form.

He showed me how to make music, how to make it big, and how to make it accessible.

Without that role modelling, I genuinely wouldn't be doing what I'm doing now. And I don't think a number of kids who grew up in Newcastle would be either.

On singing at Prince Philip's funeral …

Miriam: When the Duke of Edinburgh passed away, there were COVID protocols regarding social distancing, including allowing only three singers to perform at one time.

For the funeral, it was decided at the highest levels of government that they could indeed have four singers.

And so, the director of music, who at the time lived in a house behind mine, came round and spoke to me through the window and asked if I would do the service.

I'd been sworn to secrecy, but I said to the powers that be, "Is it possible I could just let my dad know?"

Christopher: It was huge for me to watch Miriam, for a whole lot of reasons.

Queen Elizabeth and Prince Philip were important figures in Christopher Allan's household. (ABC Newcastle: Sofie Wainwright)

I emigrated here from England at the age of seven. So, it's interesting to me that Mim has gone back and lived there, when my parents came to Australia to give my siblings and me a better life.

The queen and Prince Philip were very important figures in our house.

It's that kind of level of pride and enjoyment, and just the sheer thought of, "We're from Newcastle; things like this don't happen."

For Miriam to take part in that was a huge honour for her.

On keeping musically connected across continents

Miriam: We do talk a lot, especially about music and music education, because I'm a music educator too. We send each other articles that we read or things that we find interesting, and we talk about students a lot.

Christopher: Until COVID put a dent in things, we'd see each other every 18 months or so.

Miriam: It's not uncommon, when I come back to Australia or when Dad comes to the UK, for me to sit poor old Dad at a piano, hand him a whole stack of music, and say: "Off we go."

On being father and daughter on stage …

Christopher: If any of my children wanted to do something and their mother had said no, they would say, "It always works with Daddy."

In the Bach cantata we'll be performing, there's a conversation where the father tells his daughter to give up drinking so much coffee, and the daughter says, "I'm not giving up my coffee."

And I can just hear my own children as teenagers going, "Yeah, whatever. We're going to do what we want anyway because it always works with Daddy."

Miriam: Coffee is the subject of this cantata, but the disagreement between father and daughter could be replaced with just about anything.

But the hilarious thing is that Dad loves coffee and I cannot stand the stuff.

I do love a cup of tea, though. So, if anyone out there wants to bring me a cuppa, I probably won't say no.

This interview has been edited for clarity.

Christopher and Miriam Allan will be performing with Bach Akademie Australia from August 5–16 in Brisbane, Newcastle, Sydney, Canberra and Glenbrook.

title: Hens moved indoors but free-range label still allowed
text:
The consumer watchdog has extended its pause on free-range egg labelling enforcement as some farmers move hens indoors to protect them from H5 bird flu on state government advice.

Usually eggs can only be labelled as free range if producers meet several requirements for hens, including access to outdoors and stocking densities of no more than 10,000 hens per hectare.

As bird flu cases continue to rise, the Australian Consumer and Competition Commission (ACCC) is allowing farmers to keep chickens indoors and still use free-range cartons.

Under law, eggs labelled free range usually have to come from hens able to roam and forage outdoors. (Supplied: Providore Farm)

But ACCC deputy chair, Mick Keogh, said producers needed to let consumers know what's going on.

"If they've got their birds housed, there's an obligation to communicate that, particularly to retailers, but also more widely, to the consumers," he said.

Poultry still free of H5

H5 hasn't spread to poultry or the agriculture industry in Australia yet, but Mr Keogh said the risk was increasing.

"The spread in wild bird populations is continuing to grow … that suggests to us that the threat or the risk for domestic poultry, in particular, is growing," he said.

In early July, the ACCC confirmed it would not take enforcement action for breaches of free-range egg labelling standards, as voluntary housing measures started.

Mr Keogh said that would continue, for now.

"We don't see the situation has changed; in fact, if anything, [it] has become more urgent."

No timeframe has been set for an end to the enforcement pause.

Zac Jeffries and his wife Alana would like temporary labels to be used on cartons. (Supplied: Providore Farm)

Pasture-raised egg farm, Providore Farm, sits on the outskirts of Portland, in south-west Victoria, near where several infected greater crested terns were found.

Owner Zac Jeffries said he did not have an indoor option for his birds at the moment, and he was concerned about misleading egg labelling.

"I definitely don't like the idea that someone can be marketing their eggs as free range when they're not actually living like that," he said.

He wants to see temporary label changes, allowing farmers to use the same cartons.

"There's a two to three month wait to get a carton in … and when we do a minimum order, it's 60,000 cartons.

"It really wouldn't be hard to have a sticker or something that we applied to our carton saying, 'Temporarily inside due to government order' or 'during this outbreak.'"

Mr Jeffries said bigger farms should be able to make necessary changes.

"I don't think they should be able to continue just pumping out cartons of eggs, calling them free range when the birds are locked in for two or three months at a time."

State governments have made voluntary orders urging poultry farmers to protect flocks from infection. (Supplied: Providore Farm)

Mr Keogh acknowledged the enforcement pause may be confusing for consumers and farmers alike.

"Consumers do want to trust what they're being told and make sure it's right," he said.

"We [also] acknowledge completely that to get a box run of some thousands of egg cartons and get the labels changed is a very expensive thing."

But he said the longer the outbreak continued, it was important that free-range producers "make efforts to communicate the reality of the situation".

"Advising retailers, for example, that they may want to put signs on the shelf saying, 'In the current situation, some of these birds may have been kept in housing, and it may not be free range,'" Mr Keogh said.

Mick Keogh says free range egg farmers need to let consumers know if their hens are kept inside. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Mandatory orders on table

Voluntary housing orders are in place in several states, including in South Australia, where the bulk of the country's confirmed H5 cases are.

SA's chief vet, Dr Skye Fruean, said it was a "very dynamic situation and we are remaining really closely engaged with our poultry sector."

She said a mandatory housing order was not in place yet, but was being considered.

"It is an option open to jurisdictions at the end of the day to make their own decisions," she said.

Once state authorities declare mandatory orders for egg and chicken meat farmers to keep birds indoors, the ACCC's enforcement pause is limited to 90 days.

title: Haugset goes it alone to claim Tour de France Femmes third stage
text:
Sigrid Haugset has set off on a long solo run and kept going to the finish to win the third stage of the Women's Tour de France and claim the yellow jersey.

The Norwegian rider made her break with more than half of the tough 156.5-kilometre route between Geneva and Poligny to go.

The stage featured four categorised climbs and Haugset made her move with 85 kilometres left, at the foot of the category two Col de la Savine.

Haugset was also first across the last listed climb of the day, the category four Côte de Chaux-Champagny, followed by Lotte Kopecky about 30 seconds behind, and a nine-rider group more than two minutes adrift.

Previous yellow jersey holder Lorena Wiebes, who won the first two stages, was 13 minutes behind with the main bunch at the time. She ultimately finished more than 20 minutes adrift of Haugset and dropped to 67th in the general classification.

It was a battle between two riders going into the last 10 kilometres. Kopecky had cut Haugset's lead to 15 seconds and the Belgian rider could just about see her rival ahead.

But Haugset, sensing the danger, stood on her pedals to stay ahead and managed to increase her lead again, finishing 1:24 ahead of Kopecky.

Haugset leads the general classification by 2:02 from Kimberley Le Court of Mauritius, with 2023 Tour champion Demi Vollering third, a further four seconds behind.

This edition of the race, the fifth of the Women's Tour, covers 1,175 kilometres over nine days.

Ivan Cleary may need to wait until 2030 to coach NSW after it was revealed Matt King’s two-year contract includes an option to activate a third year should the Blues beat Queensland in 2027 or 2028. King was officially unveiled as Laurie Daley’s successor as NSW Blues coach at NSW Rugby League’s Sydney Olympic Park headquarters on Tuesday. Loading Joined by his wife Kirsten and three young daughters, King revealed he had missed out on the top job with the Blues two years ago, and said he would call on coaching heavyweights Craig Bellamy, Craig Fitzgibbon, Michael Maguire and Trent Robinson as his unofficial “advisory board”. King also said he had wanted former Storm teammate and current Maroons coach Billy Slater to be the first to hear the news of his appointment, and insisted he was under no illusions about the media scrutiny that is certain to come his way in the role.

NSWRL CEO Dave Trodden confirmed King’s job would be a full-time role and that he would automatically trigger an extension for 2029 if he led the state to Origin glory in the next two years. Panthers coach Cleary will finish up with Penrith at the end of next year and has already spoken about his hopes of coaching at representative level, leading to speculation he would be installed as Blues coach as early as 2028. Matt King was officially unveiled as NSW Blues coach on Tuesday. Add the chicken, skin side down, and cook for 4-6 minutes or until the skin is deep golden and crisp. Turn and cook for a further 4 minutes or until cooked through. Transfer to a plate, cover loosely with aluminium foil to retain heat and leave to rest before slicing thickly crosswise.

Step 2 Place 2 tablespoons of the remaining oil and the garlic into a large, deep frying pan over medium-low heat. Season with a pinch of salt and cook, stirring occasionally, for 3-4 minutes or until fragrant and lightly golden.

Step 3 Meanwhile, cook the pasta in a large saucepan of boiling salted water for 6-8 minutes or until al dente. Reserve ½ cup of the pasta cooking water, then drain.

Step 4 Add the drained pasta, reserved cooking water, chilli flakes, parsley, half the lemon zest and half the lemon juice to the garlic oil. Toss vigorously over low heat for 1-2 minutes until the liquid emulsifies into a glossy sauce that coats the pasta. Season to taste.

A Supreme Court judge has dismissed complaints from an Osborne Park private hospital that a gym operating above its premises is too noisy and impacts their medical procedures, leaving the hospital facing a hefty bill for legal costs and compensation for the gym’s loss of business. Perth Day Hospital filed a statement of claim in the Supreme Court of WA against Fitness Cartel in June, alleging that, since the gym opened last November, it had caused excessive noise both from the sound of music and dropped weights, which reverberated through the hospital’s ceiling. Fitness Cartel opened in November, and its downstairs neighbours say it’s caused problems for them ever since. Fitness Cartel The businesses share a building at 454 Scarborough Beach Road, with the fitness centre located above the hospital. Perth Day Hospital, which had seen a $16 million fit-out, was granted an urgent injunction against the gym ahead of the hospital’s planned opening on June 2, limiting the gym’s activities between 6.30am and 8pm to low music and prohibiting the use of weights including medicine balls and kettlebells.

Advertisement

The gym originally argued against the injunction, saying it had lost $15,000 due to the restrictions as well as the confidence of its members. However, the judge upheld the restrictions until the outcome of a trial examining the issue. As part of that trial, Supreme Court Justice Michael Lundberg visited the site where the gym and hospital operated. Perth Day Hospital claimed it experienced repeated “vibrations” immediately above or near treatment areas “caused by heavier weights being dropped”. The hospital offers endoscopy and pain management procedures that involve “the insertion of needles into the spine or nerves of patients”. Fitness Cartel describes itself as “a complete health and wellness destination” that includes a functional training zone and Hyrox studio.

Advertisement

It opened its doors in November and complaints about the noise began soon after. They tried to settle the matter with the gym owners by emailing them regarding the constant vibration, which they claimed was “unacceptable” and impacting their business. Perth Day Hospital in Osborne Park. Perth Day Hospital They also employed a “vibration expert” to compile a report on the impact of the noise. At the trial, Perth Day Hospital’s lawyer Martin Bennett said the worst case of recorded weight-dropping from the gym exceeded noise regulations by between 5 and 15 decibels.

Advertisement

“The vibrations were as such that cardboard office files fell from the desk, an electronic clock fixture fell from the ceiling … it’s not a case of undue sensitivity,” Bennett said. Related Article Exclusive

Courts The $16m Osborne Park hospital, the gym upstairs, and the battle over dropped weights Bennett argued the gym’s use of the building was not “ordinary and common”, and there were no other gyms in similar positions anywhere around the Scarborough Beach Road location. However, defence lawyer Simon Davis argued the hospital should never have moved into the building in the first place, and the gym was more likely to be located at the strata than the hospital. “For a building that has had many gyms in it in the past to the point where it used to be a sports centre… and used to have gyms until about 10 or 12 years ago now, [having a gym] is a common and ordinary use of the land,” he said.

“Clearly it is inappropriate to put a hospital that specialises in those procedures and only those procedures into that building in the first place.” Both parties will return to court later this month to discuss whether there will be an inquiry in regards to the costs to be paid.

ASX listed Critica Limited has landed another significant processing breakthrough at its massive Jupiter rare earths project near Mount Magnet in Western Australia’s Mid West, confirming a 30 per cent reduction in sulphuric acid consumption that could materially reduce future operating costs. The result marks another milestone in the company’s methodical campaign to strip costs out of the development of the 1.8-billion-tonne Jupiter project, Australia’s largest clay-hosted rare earths resource. Field activities at Critica Limited’s flagship Jupiter rare earths project near Yalgoo in Western Australia’s Mid-West. Testwork confirmed acid consumption could be reduced to approximately one tonne of sulphuric acid per tonne of feed, down from the previous design basis of 1.4–1.6 tonnes. Management says the result strengthens the technical case for Jupiter as it finalises the project’s highly anticipated scoping study for release in the third quarter of 2026. Independent programmes by the Australian Nuclear Science and Technology Organisation (ANSTO), GAVAQ and Australian Minmet Metallurgical Laboratories (AMML) all produced comparable outcomes. The consistent results provide confidence the lower acid consumption can be achieved under optimised conditions. At the same time, strong rare earths extraction rates were maintained, demonstrating the lower acid consumption did not come at the expense of metallurgical performance.

Advertisement

‘With optimisation now demonstrated we continue to strengthen the technical foundations of Jupiter as we finalise the Scoping Study.’ Critica Limited chief executive officer Jacob Deysel Today’s announcement is the latest win in a carefully sequenced optimisation campaign designed to attack every major cost centre in the Jupiter processing flowsheet. Critica has already demonstrated about 95 per cent mass rejection during beneficiation, boosted magnet rare earths oxide (MagREO) recovery to about 81 per cent and achieved a fourteen-fold upgrade to an intermediate concentrate grading about 3 per cent total rare earth oxides (TREO). The latest breakthrough extends that progression by reducing downstream reagent consumption. In simple terms, Critica’s strategy means that for every 100 tonnes of material mined, only about five tonnes may need to pass through the full chemical treatment process. The acid reduction makes processing the valuable five-tonne fraction even cheaper. Sulphuric acid is one of the biggest operating cost drivers in rare earths processing. Lower reagent consumption has the potential to reduce transport, handling and processing costs, improving future project economics. The company’s beneficiate-first development strategy aims to shrink the downstream chemical plant, reduce reagent use and deliver a simpler, lower-cost development.

Advertisement

Critica Limited chief executive officer Jacob Deysel said: “Our approach has been to systematically optimise each stage of the Jupiter processing flowsheet and these latest results represent another important step in that programme.” The company will now continue hydrometallurgical optimisation and validation testwork while refining acid bake operating conditions and reagent consumption across varying feed grades. The latest metallurgical results will feed into downstream process optimisation, product qualification and the engineering work underpinning the Jupiter Scoping Study. The work is designed to further refine the processing flowsheet as management advances the Jupiter development programme. With the project’s geology already well defined, management’s focus is now on proving the processing route can consistently deliver competitive operating costs at commercial scale. Each successive optimisation removes another layer of technical uncertainty as management works to convert Jupiter from a geological success into a development project. Jupiter benefits from relatively low uranium and thorium levels, a characteristic that could simplify permitting, residue management and customer acceptance compared with some hard-rock rare earths deposits. Its more lucrative electric engine magnet rare earths inventory is well positioned to benefit from long-term demand driven by electric vehicles, robotics, artificial intelligence infrastructure, wind turbines and advanced defence technologies. Critica’s work is unfolding against a backdrop of growing government support for Australia’s domestic critical minerals processing sector. Federal and state policy initiatives are aimed at securing sovereign supply chains and encouraging lower-cost, Western-aligned rare earths production.

Advertisement

While Jupiter remains the company’s flagship project, Critica’s other key project is the Mt Lindsay tin and tungsten project in Tasmania, broadening its exposure beyond rare earths. The complementary asset is also essential to advanced manufacturing, electronics and defence, giving the company leverage to another suite of critical minerals. With a string of processing victories now under its belt, Critica is steadily transforming Jupiter from a not well-understood but giant rare earths discovery into what is shaping as a potentially commercially credible development project. The upcoming scoping study now looms large on the horizon as the company’s biggest test yet, showing whether its systematic processing improvements can convert immense geological scale into competitive project economics. title: Amplia teams up with big pharma for lung cancer trial
text:
