Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"We won gold, felt like it was ages ago now," said his teammate Lachlan Kennedy.

The holdup was the result of Canada's protests over their initial disqualification for a supposed illegal changeover, which was first upheld and then deliberated upon by the jury at great length until Canada was cleared for the silver.

It was an unusual conclusion to Australia's most successful athletics day ever at the Games, with a record haul of seven gold medals and 17 medals in total, including two events where the Aussies swept the podium.

Australia's previous record was set more than 70 years ago, with six gold medals and 11 medals in total in 1950.

It capped off the penultimate day of a stripped-back Games that had been quirky from the outset.

Why were these Games different?

Victoria was originally supposed to host, but withdrew in 2023 due to rising costs. At the time, it prompted some to question the relevance of the Games and whether the event had a future at all.

The following year, organisers announced that Glasgow would step in as host city, with its Games to be supported in part by money from Victoria. The Victorian government had to pay a compensation of $589m including a $380 million settlement to cancel its hosting obligations.

While the Games has always had fewer sports and athletes than the Olympics, the 2026 event was even more pared back.

Glasgow hosted the Commonwealth Games on a tighter budget after Victoria pulled out in 2023. Source: Getty / Ross MacDonald/SNS Group

The 2022 Birmingham Games featured 20 sports and more than 5,000 athletes, while Glasgow hosted just 3,000 athletes competing in ten sports.

Some onlookers said the vibes in the city were vastly different to 2014, when it last hosted the Games.

Michael Gleeson, sports columnist for the Nine newspapers, said the event was winnowed back so far "that in Glasgow, you barely know the Games are on".

Australia's moments to remember

In its blockbuster final day, the Australian athletics team secured two podium sweeps — first in the women's 10,000m race walk thanks to one-two-three finishes by Jemima Montag, Elizabeth McMillen and Rebecca Henderson, then in the women's mile with Abbey Caldwell, Jessica Hull and Claudia Hollingsworth.

Ending a 52-year drought, Kennedy, Azzopardi, Calab Law and Rohan Browning were the first to win gold for Australia in the men's 4x100 relay since 1974.

Kurtis Marschall pulled off a three-peat in the pole vault, nabbing his third consecutive gold and setting a new Games record of 5.85m.

Jemima Montag, Elizabeth McMillen and Rebecca Henderson took out gold, silver and bronze for Australia in the 10,000m race walk. Source: Getty / Michael Steele

"I'm planning on never quitting. I want to do this forever and go to every Comm Games ever. Let’s keep it rolling," he said afterwards.

Earlier in the week, Australia dominated in the pool, setting its own new record haul of 37 gold, 16 silver and 23 bronze medals.

Kyle Chalmers earned his tenth Commonwealth Games gold, topping Ian Thorpe as Australia's most successful male swimmer at the event.

In the gym, Georgia Godwin became Australia's most decorated female Commonwealth Games gymnast, staging a remarkable comeback after an injury dashed her hopes of competing at the Paris Olympics.

Heading into the final day of this year's Games, Australia was leading the medal board with 65 gold medals, 41 silver and 52 bronze.

The ones that got people talking

The late-night medal ceremony wasn't the only unusual moment of the Games.

The opening ceremony was full of flair, featuring flaming teacakes, bedazzled unicorns and King Charles emerging from a TARDIS — a time machine made famous by the British sci-fi show Doctor Who.

While the 2026 Games attracted less attention than previous events, they still had their share of memorable moments, drama, and unusual decisions.

Felicity Wilson-Haffenden was controversially disqualified from her bronze medal race over strapping on her shoulder. Source: Getty / Molly Darlington

Australian cyclist Felicity Wilson-Haffenden was disqualified from her bronze medal race after officials ruled shoulder tape she was wearing for an injury caused a "morphological change".

Officials deemed the tape worn beneath her racing suit breached a rule prohibiting clothing or accessories from altering a rider's physical profile.

The decision sparked controversy and confusion because Wilson-Haffenden had worn tape on the same shoulder a day earlier without issue while helping Australia win gold in the women's team pursuit.

Eliza Ault-Connell won bronze in a re-run after a crash in the women's 1,500m T54 final set off a series of appeals. Source: Getty / Martin Rickett

Another race that got people talking was the women's T54 1,500m final, which saw four crashes, three overturned wheelchairs, a disqualification and a series of appeals. Officials then decided the race would be held again nearly 40 hours later.

Australia’s Eliza Ault-Connell, who was caught up in the crash and successfully protested, ended up nabbing bronze in the re-run.

title: Federal efforts died, but another Australian state has committed to forming a truth-telling body
text:
In brief South Australia will follow Victoria on the Uluru Statement's agenda.

Acting Premier Kyam Maher says the commitment pre-dates the failed 2023 referendum and stands apart from it.

South Australia will stand up a truth-telling commission over coming months, extending a Voice-to-treaty framework that cements the state as the second-most advanced jurisdiction on the Uluru Statement's unfinished agenda.

Speaking to NITV's John-Paul Janke and Natalie Ahmat on the broadcaster's Garma set, against a backdrop of stringybarks rising from the red Arnhem Land dirt, Acting Premier Kyam Maher said the state government would spend $8.5 million on a commission that will run a truth-telling process and advise on a possible treaty.

Maher is also South Australia's Aboriginal Affairs Minister.

The commission is the next stage in a program South Australian Labor has pursued since 2019. Responding to the Uluru Statement from the Heart — the 2017 declaration by Indigenous leaders calling for a Voice to Parliament, treaty and truth-telling — was among the party's first commitments, made in opposition that year.

Labor won government in 2022 and legislated the state's Voice to Parliament in March 2023. It has held power since, winning a second term earlier this year.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The federal Voice to Parliament suffered a major setback in October 2023, when just over 60 per cent of Australians rejected a constitutional referendum to recognise Indigenous people and establish a national advisory body, with every state and territory except the ACT voting No.

After Queensland, South Australia recorded the country's highest No vote.

A promise predating the No vote

South Australia though, had already legislated its own Voice to Parliament before the referendum. Maher rejected the argument the No result should halt the state's plans.

"This is about something we committed seven years ago to do in South Australia, and we will take that commitment," he told NITV on Sunday, referencing the 2019 pledge Labor made in opposition and carried into government.

"What was voted on at the referendum was to change the federal constitution, to firstly recognise Aboriginal people — recognise the oldest living culture this planet's ever seen — but also to establish an advisory body."

READ MORE Diplomacy and dance as international Indigenous communities connect at Garma

He acknowledged not everyone was behind him. "I wouldn't say there's no division," Maher said, adding that the issue still generates dozens of letters to his office each month.

The state's Voice has now been through two elections, in 2024 and 2026.

The body — comprising 12 members drawn from six regional bodies, all elected by and from First Nations South Australians — advises parliament and government on health, education, justice and other matters affecting their communities.

Maher said the first part of the state's efforts was spent building the machinery of a body. Without a national precedent, he likened the work to "building the plane as you're flying it".

"[You're] having to put that infrastructure around something that had never happened in Australia before," he said.

At the second election, about half the incumbents were returned and half the seats went to new members, a mix he said was beginning to produce substantive advice for the government to act on.

Maher casts the truth-telling commission as "the next element" of the same work.

On Saturday, Voice architect Noel Pearson used his first major speech since the referendum to reckon with the defeat, asking what right anyone had to offer a vision that turned out to be a "mirage" — a measure of how heavily the 2023 loss still hangs over national debate.

The map beyond Canberra

South Australia's trajectory places it just behind Victoria, which commenced Australia's first treaty under its Statewide Treaty Act in May.

The law makes Victoria's First Peoples' Assembly a permanent body, known as Gellung Warl. It is a new truth-telling institution that builds on the earlier Yoorrook Justice Commission.

Other states have not been able to replicate South Australia and Victoria's successes.

Queensland repealed its Path to Treaty laws in late 2024, shutting down a truth-telling inquiry barely five months into its work and abolishing the body set up to negotiate treaty.

The Northern Territory's Country Liberal government scrapped its long-running treaty process in early 2025.

New South Wales is midway through a 12-month consultation on whether Aboriginal communities want a treaty at all, while Western Australia has pursued truth-telling and redress rather than a treaty.

Maher also welcomed the Australian Electoral Commission's decision to rename the federal seat of Grey as the Division of O'Donoghue in July. On Sunday, the Acting Premier said doing so honoured a South Australian in the late Yankunytjatjara leader Lowitja O'Donoghue.

The electorate takes in much of the Anangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara Lands.

Maher, who knew O'Donoghue, called the change "exceptionally significant". It also points to a history in which "Aboriginal people have been deliberately excluded".

The unveiling in June of a bronze statue of O'Donoghue at Tarntanya Wama (Elder Park) in Adelaide — the first of six planned to honour prominent Aboriginal South Australians — is part of the same effort to correct that record.

title: How this tiny Spanish city became a global migration flashpoint
text:
In brief More than 50,000 migrants crossed into Ceuta, with most returning to Morocco within 48 hours.

Spain says a new barrier will help prevent further crossings at a key entry point.

A tiny Spanish territory on the northern tip of Africa has become the focus of international attention — and debate — after more than 50,000 migrants crossed into it in a mass rush that left at least 67 people dead.

The European Union will hold crisis talks after the mass crossing into Ceuta on Thursday. Most of the migrants had returned to Morocco within 48 hours of crossing, but the incident has raised alarm among European leaders about the bloc's shared border security.

Ceuta has steadily fortified its border over the years as it became a key route for migrants trying to reach Europe.

The Spanish exclave already had a border fence with Morocco, but Spanish authorities have since begun installing a 500m-long floating barrier on its sea border with its African neighbour.

It's designed to stand 30 to 70cm above water and extend as much as one metre below the surface, while a channel between the barriers will allow Civil Guard vessels to patrol the area, the government said.

The arrivals were equivalent to nearly two-thirds of Ceuta's permanent population of about 83,000.

How and why did the migrants enter?

Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish exclave on the North African coast, are the only two land borders between the European Union and Africa.

Many arrivals swam to Ceuta around the Tarajal breakwater — a sea wall extending out from the Spain-Morocco border into the Mediterranean — to come ashore at Tarajal beach.

READ MORE The Spanish territory at the centre of a unique migration challenge

"Spain gives you the chance to make your future, not like Morocco," Buji, a 21-year-old Moroccan who is studying to be a teacher, told the Associated Press (AP). "I am a talented boy. I just want a chance."

He said he lost his belongings and money in the crossing, and when he realised that he would likely face legal limbo and detention, he turned back.

"I’ve spent perhaps 14 years studying, but there’s nothing at home, and I'd have to work 12-hour shifts for a meagre wage," he told AP.

"That’s why I came here, but I haven’t found any opportunities here either, so I have to go back."

To reach the city, migrants have been known to swim around 5km from the Moroccan town of Fnideq.

Officials said at least 67 bodies were recovered on the Spanish side after some migrants drowned and others were crushed while trying to climb the breakwater and border fence.

Many were driven to migrate by economic hardship and reportedly by rumours circulating on Moroccan social media that border security had been relaxed.

Spanish interior minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska blamed people-smuggling networks for exploiting vulnerable migrants by spreading misleading interpretations of a recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling.

Spain's immigration policies

Spain's 29 June Supreme Court ruling said authorities cannot summarily deport migrants who arrive by sea without due process, because they did not cross the physical border barriers referenced in Spanish law.

Gemma Pinyol-Jiménez, head of migration policies and diversity at Instrategies and an associate researcher at GRITIM–Pompeu Fabra University, told CNN that it effectively means migrants can't be pushed back at sea because there is no crossing of a formal border.

It does not mean people cannot be sent back, and the deportation process can still be completed within days.

"The idea is to facilitate the work of the police, but it doesn’t mean these people can stay in Ceuta," she said.

In contrast to much of Europe, Spain has adopted a less restrictive stance on migrants, introducing a program to grant residency to more than half a million undocumented people already living there.

Experts have said that summer sea conditions, Spain's relatively strong economy, and its immigration policies may have contributed to the surge in migrant arrivals.

How have world leaders responded?

The mass crossing triggered alarm across the European Union.

Leaders of Italy, Denmark, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, the Netherlands, Poland, Romania, Slovenia, Slovakia and Sweden signed a letter asking the EU’s current Irish presidency to convene a video conference of interior ministers.

"We cannot allow uncontrolled mass crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration or other hybrid threats to create the perception that illegal entry into the European Union is possible. That a migrant’s illegal entry can turn into legal stay," the letter said.

The meeting has been scheduled for Tuesday.

Italy announced on Friday it was suspending its Schengen arrangements with Spain for a month in response to the incident.

The Schengen agreement allows passport-free travel between 29 European countries.

Thousands of migrants crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in north Africa, many of them by swimming. Source: Getty / Marcos Moreno

"This is an extraordinary measure, adopted to safeguard national security and prevent possible repercussions for our nation," Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, a right-wing leader who campaigned on a pledge to reduce illegal immigration, wrote on X.

Italy, which does not share a land border with Spain, also said it had agreed with France to strengthen controls along their border to try to prevent undocumented migrants from crossing.

Spain's centre-left prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, criticised the decision as "selfish, polarising and unlawful".

United States President Donald Trump, whose mass immigration crackdowns have been a key pillar of his second term, held a cabinet meeting about what he called a "catastrophe" and what "looks like an invasion" in Spain.

"That same thing is going to happen to us if the Republicans don’t get elected," he said.

Dozens of people died while attempting to cross into Ceuta. Source: Getty / Europa Press News

Spain said migrants who entered Ceuta irregularly would not be allowed to travel onwards to mainland Spain or elsewhere in the Schengen area.

It said order had been restored within 24 hours and that reinforced police and military deployments would remain for as long as necessary.

Migrants return

Hundreds of migrants continued to make their way back to Morocco on Saturday, some saying they had done so voluntarily, leaving Ceuta after what they described as degrading treatment on the Spanish side of the border.

They walked along a long stretch of beach before slipping into Morocco through a small breach in the border fence.

"I decided to come back on my own," Ouail Lamzeiz told AP.

"I spent eight days in Ceuta, and I was about to get a bed at the migrant centre, but I hadn’t eaten for days. Even the Moroccans there didn't help."

Migrants told AP they spent their nights sleeping in the forests around Ceuta because they could not find shelter, and that they often fought over food.

Others have said they do not intend to return.

Mohamed Hatri, a 23-year-old Moroccan, said he was determined to stay.

"They've closed everything down so that we can’t buy anything to eat, to force us to return to our country," he told AP.

A Supreme Court judge has dismissed complaints from an Osborne Park private hospital that a gym operating above its premises is too noisy and impacts their medical procedures, leaving the hospital facing a hefty bill for legal costs and compensation for the gym’s loss of business. title: Critica slashes key cost at WA flagship rare earths project
text:
Advertisement

Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Critica slashes key cost at WA flagship rare earths project Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Penny Taylor August 4, 2026 — 12:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

ASX listed Critica Limited has landed another significant processing breakthrough at its massive Jupiter rare earths project near Mount Magnet in Western Australia’s Mid West, confirming a 30 per cent reduction in sulphuric acid consumption that could materially reduce future operating costs. The result marks another milestone in the company’s methodical campaign to strip costs out of the development of the 1.8-billion-tonne Jupiter project, Australia’s largest clay-hosted rare earths resource. Field activities at Critica Limited’s flagship Jupiter rare earths project near Yalgoo in Western Australia’s Mid-West. Testwork confirmed acid consumption could be reduced to approximately one tonne of sulphuric acid per tonne of feed, down from the previous design basis of 1.4–1.6 tonnes. Management says the result strengthens the technical case for Jupiter as it finalises the project’s highly anticipated scoping study for release in the third quarter of 2026. Independent programmes by the Australian Nuclear Science and Technology Organisation (ANSTO), GAVAQ and Australian Minmet Metallurgical Laboratories (AMML) all produced comparable outcomes. The consistent results provide confidence the lower acid consumption can be achieved under optimised conditions. At the same time, strong rare earths extraction rates were maintained, demonstrating the lower acid consumption did not come at the expense of metallurgical performance.

Advertisement

‘With optimisation now demonstrated we continue to strengthen the technical foundations of Jupiter as we finalise the Scoping Study.’ Critica Limited chief executive officer Jacob Deysel Today’s announcement is the latest win in a carefully sequenced optimisation campaign designed to attack every major cost centre in the Jupiter processing flowsheet. Critica has already demonstrated about 95 per cent mass rejection during beneficiation, boosted magnet rare earths oxide (MagREO) recovery to about 81 per cent and achieved a fourteen-fold upgrade to an intermediate concentrate grading about 3 per cent total rare earth oxides (TREO). The latest breakthrough extends that progression by reducing downstream reagent consumption. In simple terms, Critica’s strategy means that for every 100 tonnes of material mined, only about five tonnes may need to pass through the full chemical treatment process. The acid reduction makes processing the valuable five-tonne fraction even cheaper. Sulphuric acid is one of the biggest operating cost drivers in rare earths processing. Lower reagent consumption has the potential to reduce transport, handling and processing costs, improving future project economics. The company’s beneficiate-first development strategy aims to shrink the downstream chemical plant, reduce reagent use and deliver a simpler, lower-cost development.

Advertisement

Critica Limited chief executive officer Jacob Deysel said: “Our approach has been to systematically optimise each stage of the Jupiter processing flowsheet and these latest results represent another important step in that programme.” The company will now continue hydrometallurgical optimisation and validation testwork while refining acid bake operating conditions and reagent consumption across varying feed grades. The latest metallurgical results will feed into downstream process optimisation, product qualification and the engineering work underpinning the Jupiter Scoping Study. The work is designed to further refine the processing flowsheet as management advances the Jupiter development programme. With the project’s geology already well defined, management’s focus is now on proving the processing route can consistently deliver competitive operating costs at commercial scale. Each successive optimisation removes another layer of technical uncertainty as management works to convert Jupiter from a geological success into a development project. Jupiter benefits from relatively low uranium and thorium levels, a characteristic that could simplify permitting, residue management and customer acceptance compared with some hard-rock rare earths deposits. Its more lucrative electric engine magnet rare earths inventory is well positioned to benefit from long-term demand driven by electric vehicles, robotics, artificial intelligence infrastructure, wind turbines and advanced defence technologies. Critica’s work is unfolding against a backdrop of growing government support for Australia’s domestic critical minerals processing sector. Federal and state policy initiatives are aimed at securing sovereign supply chains and encouraging lower-cost, Western-aligned rare earths production.

Advertisement

While Jupiter remains the company’s flagship project, Critica’s other key project is the Mt Lindsay tin and tungsten project in Tasmania, broadening its exposure beyond rare earths. The complementary asset is also essential to advanced manufacturing, electronics and defence, giving the company leverage to another suite of critical minerals. With a string of processing victories now under its belt, Critica is steadily transforming Jupiter from a not well-understood but giant rare earths discovery into what is shaping as a potentially commercially credible development project. title: Amplia teams up with big pharma for lung cancer trial
text:
Advertisement

Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Amplia teams up with big pharma for lung cancer trial Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward August 4, 2026 — 12:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Melbourne-based ASX listed biotech Amplia Therapeutics has secured a major collaboration with pharmaceutical goliath Eli Lilly & Company to evaluate a new combination therapy aimed at tackling non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The two companies have signed a Clinical Trial Collaboration and Supply Agreement that will see Amplia’s investigational FAK blocker drug known as “narmafotinib” trialled in combination with Eli Lilly’s late-stage KRAS G12C inhibitor, “olomorasib”. Melbourne-based biotech Amplia Therapeutics is collaborating with Eli Lilly & Company to trial its narmafotinib FAK blocker drug for non-small cell lung cancer. The Phase 1b/2b clinical trial will assess the safety and efficacy of the novel combination as a second-line treatment for patients with advanced-stage NSCLC. Under the deal Amplia will conduct the study at sites across Australia and the US. Notably, Eli Lilly will provide its olomorasib drug for the trial at no cost.

Advertisement

′ The combination of FAK and KRAS inhibition can lead to improved outcomes.′ Amplia Therapeutics chief executive officer and managing director Dr Chris Burns While the trial is slated to begin in late 2026, the two companies will now start collaborating to finalise the clinical study protocol and other associated documents, building on an advanced draft they have already developed together. The collaboration is a significant step for Amplia, extending the clinical reach of its lead drug beyond its established programs in pancreatic and ovarian cancer into the lucrative NSCLC market. That market is currently valued at about US$31 billion (A$44 billion) and is forecast to grow to more than US$60 billion (A$86 billion) by 2033. The trial will specifically target a patient subset with “KRAS G12C” mutations, which the company says occurs in about 13 per cent of NSCLC patients and between 1 and 3 per cent of those with other solid tumours. FAK is a protein inside cells that acts like a control switch for movement, survival and attachment. It sits where cells anchor to their surrounding environment and helps tell them whether to grow, move or shut down.

Advertisement

In many cancers, FAK becomes overactive or over-produced, helping tumour cells survive, move and spread. That has made it a target for cancer-fighting drugs such as narmafotinib. The company says the scientific theory underpinning the trial is that the FAK activation process is a key driver of resistance to KRAS G12C inhibitors, a class of drugs that has shown promise but often only sees short-lived benefits. By combining a FAK blocker like narmafotinib with a KRAS inhibitor, the companies are hoping to overcome this resistance and deliver a more durable and effective treatment. Lilly’s confidence in its own drug, olomorasib, is evident, with the pharma giant already advancing it in two separate global Phase 3 trials. Amplia chief executive officer and managing director Dr Chris Burns said: “This collaboration is an exciting new stage in the clinical progression of narmafotinib. We and others have shown that the combination of FAK and KRAS inhibition can lead to improved outcomes, and we are excited to advance with this clinical study to explore the combination potential with olomorasib, Eli Lilly’s leading KRAS G12C inhibitor currently undergoing two global Phase 3 studies in NSCLC.” The collaboration with Lilly leverages narmafotinib’s growing base of clinical evidence. Amplia says the new study builds on promising clinical data from its “ACCENT” study in pancreatic cancer, which has shown that narmafotinib doesn’t cause any further side effects when added to chemotherapy and shows a range of compelling positive outcomes across patient responses and survival.

Advertisement

The company’s flagship ACCENT trial which tested narmafotinib with standard-of-care chemotherapy, has already delivered impressive data including a response rate of 36 per cent, a median overall survival of 11.1 months and an unprecedented complete response rate of 7.8 per cent. In addition to the ACCENT study, Amplia is also running a second pancreatic cancer trial known as AMPLICITY and is planning a third trial in ovarian cancer, dubbed PRROSE, which is scheduled to begin recruiting later this year. Impressively, Amplia has already secured significant regulatory milestones in the US, with the Food and Drug Administration granting narmafotinib Orphan Drug Designation for both pancreatic cancer and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, in addition to a Fast Track pathway for pancreatic cancer. Backing up its clinical ambitions, the company recently completed its first large-scale manufacturing campaign, producing 13 kilograms of narmafotinib’s active pharmaceutical ingredient. Amplia appears to have the right people in the room to navigate the high-stakes world of drug development too. Chief executive officer Dr Burns was a co-recipient of the 2024 Prime Minister’s Prize for Innovation and was involved in discovering the now-approved drug momelotinib.

Advertisement

Independent non-executive director Dr Robert Peach also co-founded biotech company Receptos, which was acquired by Celgene in 2015 for a staggering US$7.8 billion (A$11.1 billion). With its lead drug now being tested in pancreatic cancer and set to enter a trial for lung cancer with a global pharmaceutical leader, Amplia appears to be building a compelling case for narmafotinib as a versatile combination agent. The latest deal with Eli Lilly might just be a pivotal moment for the company, potentially thrusting the Melbourne biotech into a much larger and more lucrative arena. title: The real reason Trump just rushed to help Japan
text:
Advertisement

BusinessMarketsCurrencies Opinion The real reason Trump just rushed to help Japan Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist August 4, 2026 — 11:57am

August 4, 2026 — 11:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The joint Japanese and American intervention in currency markets to prop up the Japanese yen seems to have worked, for the moment at least. Whether it lasts is another matter. On Thursday and Friday last week, the Bank of Japan and the US Treasury were in the market, with the BoJ selling dollars to buy yen and the US selling euros, peculiarly, to add to the buying. US President Donald Trump and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in Tokyo last year. AP It’s the first time since 2011 (after the Tohoku earthquake which led to a flood of repatriated funds held offshore by Japanese investors) that the US had intervened to affect the yen’s value, although on that previous occasion it was to weaken, rather than strengthen, the currency. The BoJ and Treasury were prompted to intervene after the yen fell to 40-year lows against the dollar, despite the BoJ’s attempts to put a floor under it. With short-sellers piling in, the yen had weakened to more than 163 yen to the dollar, its weakest level since 1986.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Japan A line in the sand for the world’s largest creditor has been breached Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The BoJ spent an estimated $US53 billion ($75.7 billion) on Thursday and another $US36 billion or so on Friday, with the US support likely to have been a fraction of that in dollar terms, but far more potent in terms of the signal it sent the market. The yen is now trading around 157 yen to the dollar. Japan’s interest in strengthening its currency is obvious, America’s less so. The inexorable slide in the value of the yen has, despite unsuccessful attempts by the BoJ in April and May to arrest it, been driven by Japan’s poor fiscal position, with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi planning an expansive program of tax cuts and spending in an economy where government debt is already more than 200 per cent of GDP (albeit that about half that debt is owned by the government itself). That fiscal strategy is out of kilter with the BoJ’s monetary policy, where the bank has been cautiously edging up its policy rate, which now stands at 1 per cent, as the economy emerges from decades of stagnation.

Advertisement

With Japan’s interest differentials widening against the rest of the world, it is the currency that has had to absorb the pressure. The US Federal Reserve Board’s federal funds rate target is between 3.5 per cent and 3.75 per cent and the market expects a Fed rate rise before the end of the year – and Japanese bond yields are suppressed by the BoJ’s monetary policies (it is still buying long bonds to keep the yields low). With a growing yield differential and Japanese inflation rising, the currency has succumbed to that pressure, creating new stresses for a country reliant on imports of energy and food. The war in the Middle East has caused oil and LNG prices to soar, with the weak yen exacerbating the cost of commodities that are priced in US dollars and adding another layer to inflationary pressures and the pressure for more Japanese interest rate rises. The explanation for America’s willingness to lend its firepower and credibility to the defence of the yen is less obvious, but probably multi-layered.

Advertisement

It is almost certainly more prosaic than Donald Trump’s explanation that it was a display of friendship. The US had intervened “because we have a good relationship with Japan. We’re very strong, very strong financially. Japan’s been very good to us, with the exception, of course, of Pearl Harbour,” he said, in his usual tactless fashion. Japan’s weak fiscal position will remain weak, as will the yen, until there is structural change within the Japanese economy and financial markets. Getty Among the lesser motivations would have been concerns that a cheap yen makes Japan’s exports more competitive and could also undermine its ability to deliver on the pledge Trump extorted from it, using the threat of tariffs, to invest $US550 billion in America. More significant would be the fact that Japan is America’s biggest foreign creditor.

Advertisement

Related Article Retail ‘People want something more than value’: Why we’re so into buying Japanese stuff It holds about $US1.1 trillion of US Treasury securities. If left to defend the yen by itself, it would probably have to dump sizeable volumes of those holdings, pushing up US bond yields in a market where the US 30-year bond is already at levels last seen in 2007. For an administration facing debt levels rapidly nearing $US40 trillion, or about 123 per cent of GDP, running fiscal deficits close to 6 per cent of GDP and having to refinance about a third of its debt as it rolls over this year, that would mean even higher US interest costs. In the background is a larger threat, and not just to the US and its markets. The significant interest rate differential and persistently weak currency have made the yen a popular funding currency for hedge funds and other traders, who borrow yen to invest in higher-yielding assets elsewhere.

Advertisement

While that trade has been slightly diminished as the BoJ has inched up short-term interest rates, there are estimates that the “carry trades” still amount to more than $US1 trillion. If those were to unwind, the trillions of dollars of Japanese holdings offshore – apart from the bond holdings, Japan’s institutions hold about $US1.2 trillion of US equities and hundreds of billions of other assets – might flood back to Japan, igniting financial stresses, perhaps crises, in the markets they are exiting. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent used euros rather than the dollar as the funding currency for buying yen, in an effort to not weaken the greenback. AP Japan, the US and other central banks and governments want a controlled rather than disruptive unwinding of those trades – if the gradual normalisation of Japan’s economic settings that began under Shinzo Abe and is accelerating under Takaichi continues and rate differentials become tighter. Having decided to come to Japan’s aid, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent – a former hedge fund manager with George Soros who made a lot of money in currency trading – chose a novel approach.

Advertisement

Instead of using the dollar as the funding currency for buying yen, he used euros. And to head off a firesale of Japan’s Treasury holdings if it ran out of dollar liquidity, he convinced the Fed to increase the size of a repo facility that enables governments to get access to US dollars by using their Treasury holdings as security. The use of euros was presumably to avoid the US having to sell dollars and devaluing its own currency. The BoJ and US Treasury are buying Japan time. While Trump might like a weaker dollar to improve the competitiveness of US exports, a strong dollar is a weapon the administration has wielded, or threatened to wield, in imposing sanctions against its perceived foes. It also gives the US a unique level of influence over the world’s financial system and global trade while lowering US interest costs and raising the US standard of living relative to what it might be if the dollar weren’t the world’s reserve currency.

Advertisement

Bessent would be reluctant to jeopardise that status, hence the selling of euros (or using derivatives to effectively sell them) to buy yen. Related Article Opinion

Trump's America Fool’s gold: Trump is set to break his promise to America Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The expanded Fed line – normally, the Fed gives access to a maximum of $US60 billion a day – is another strategy for protecting the US bond market. By borrowing dollars from the Fed, using its Treasury securities as collateral, the BoJ avoids having to sell down its Treasury holdings. Interventions in currency markets tend to be briefly successful before the underlying economic and financial settings again prevail. The BoJ and US Treasury are buying Japan time, and perhaps a more orderly adjustment in the near term, but Japan’s weak fiscal position will remain weak, as will the yen, until there is structural change within the Japanese economy and financial markets. title: Chapel Street to shut 350 car parks in parking shake-up
text:
Advertisement

PoliticsVictoriaCity life Chapel Street to shut 350 car parks in parking shake-up Rachael Ward August 4, 2026 — 11:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Chapel Street is set for a parking shake-up with council voting to shut more than 350 car spots in the heart of the precinct while extending one-hour free parking near Prahran Market. Stonnington councillors voted to close the roof of the Elizabeth Street Car Park next to Prahran Market, which has 257 spots, and the roof of the King Street Car Park near Prahran Town Hall, which has 99 spots. Stonnington resident and Prahran Market trader Wendy Ali-Akil, of Stir the Pot, outside the Elizabeth Street Car Park. Photograph by Chris Hopkins The remaining 373 spaces within the Elizabeth Street Car Park will be reserved for retail customers only, with one-hour free parking available across the day, no minimum spend for validated parking and operating hours reduced to between 5am and 9pm. The roofs will be shut over the next eight weeks, while there are no plans to change existing free parking along Chapel Street.

Advertisement

Related Article Education Melbourne High students face portables, remote learning over ‘extreme’ safety concerns Councillors endorsed the changes on Monday night citing the municipality’s rising tax bill due to the extension of the state government’s congestion levy which applies to parking spots, which would cost the council $4.1 million a year under existing arrangements. The council claims there will be “no material impact” on parking availability as internal figures show the two impacted parking complexes are on average just over one-third full, while the $64 million Prahran Square Car Park could cope with extra cars during peak periods as it is on average 48 per cent full. Prahran Market trader and Stonnington resident Wendy Ali-Akil is relieved one-hour free parking will be extended throughout the day for market customers but is also disappointed hundreds of car parks will be lost in the Chapel Street precinct. “To be taking away any car spaces in the Prahran area just seems like a very short-sighted result for residents, traders and visitors to the area,” the founder of Stir The Pot food store said.

Advertisement

The roof of the Elizabeth Street Car Park is set to be rented out, with more than 250 car spots lost. Photograph by Chris Hopkins Ali-Akil is concerned existing parking rates deter shoppers from visiting Prahran Market, with parking currently costing $4.20 for visits of up to 30 minutes, $10.50 for one to two hours and $18 for three to four hours. She hopes more will be done to entice back locals who load up their cars with groceries at other markets, including nearby South Melbourne Market, which offers two hours free parking on weekdays and entries before 10am on weekends. “If the Elizabeth Street Car Park is only at one-third capacity, there’s a reason for that. It’s the prices – and I don’t agree with the state government levy, I think it’s a cash grab – but the prices are keeping people away from the car park, keeping people away from the area,” she said. She hoped council would consider offering discounted parking to traders and their staff, particularly as many workers arrive in the dark before the market’s doors open at 7am. Currently, workers can apply for reduced monthly permits which work out about $100 a week in parking costs.

Advertisement

The congestion levy is a fee charged by the State Revenue Office to all public and private off-street parking in designated inner-city areas and is designed to encourage more public transport use, with the fee expanding into parts of Stonnington as of January 2026. The council has received advice the Elizabeth Street Car Park will be eligible for a 50 per cent levy discount under the changes, which includes extra security. Stonnington Mayor Melina Sehr said the council voted to shut the car spots across the two complexes as they were underutilised. “Why would we pay a tax on them on a daily basis when they’re not being used? That’s just throwing ratepayer money away,” Sehr said.

Advertisement

“There’s nothing to be alarmed about, there’s no changes to parking arrangements apart from closing off car parks that no one’s using.” Both roofs will be empty until at least after Christmas, with the council initially considering renting out the spaces but instead deciding to monitor demand and consider opening up the car parks during the festive period if needed. Associate Professor Alexa Delbosc from Monash University’s Institute of Transport Studies said Stonnington was in a “uniquely difficult situation to cope” with the congestion levy as it is one of the few inner-city councils that does not have paid spots on major roads like Chapel Street, but does charge people to use off-street car parks. “Even without the congestion charge you still had to pay more to park in the multi-storey car parks. Why would you do that if you could just drive around and around and around looking for a free parking space?” she said.

Advertisement

“Best practice in parking demand in busy places is for the on-street parking to be more expensive than the off-street parking.” Related Article City life This hedge was their pride and joy. Then came the council email to ‘butcher’ it Delbosc doubted the council would ever consider charging for on-street parking as it could impact businesses, although the arrangement is in operation in many other inner-city spots. “For some reason, on Chapel Street, on Toorak Road, it’s free. It’s very hard to start charging for something you used to give away for free but other councils have done it.” Delbosc said she would not be surprised if the congestion levy continues to expand across Melbourne as the population grows and density increases through designated activity centres near public transport where development is encouraged.

Advertisement

Parking remains one of the most controversial issues in Stonnington and other councils, with the introduction of paid on-street parking for residents and digital permits sparking major backlash. In 2015, the battle over paid parking metres in Yarraville erupted into a violent brawl, with a 61-year-old man charged after two councillors were assaulted. A Victorian government spokesperson said council car parking decisions are a matter for local government not the state, and the congestion levy has applied to inner-Melbourne car parks for almost two decades. “Labor backs our high street traders, that’s why we introduced a 50 per cent parking concession for retail precincts just this year,” they said. title: Tested on pigs, bad data but given to ambos anyway: Homegrown defibrillator’s red flags
text:
The CellAED defibrillator was tested on pigs, not humans, before going on the market.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A whistleblower tried twice to warn Australia’s medical regulator about false claims made by a defibrillator maker, but officials took no action. It can also be revealed that the CellAED defibrillator had been tested only on two pigs when its Australian manufacturer, Rapid Response Revival, applied for approval. Yet far from restarting their hearts, the device electrocuted both animals. The developments heap fresh pressure on the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA), after this masthead’s Medical Malfunctions investigation revealed weak laws were allowing medical devices such as the CellAED to be sold with no human evidence showing they worked or were safe. The Medical Malfunctions investigation used automated website scrapers to crack open the TGA’s database and extract about 81,000 publicly available reports detailing adverse-event reports submitted to the regulator since 2012. Medical Malfunctions has already highlighted issues with the operation and regulation of devices such as glucose monitors and insulin pumps used by hundreds of thousands of Australians, spinal pain pumps and heart surgery machines. A former executive at Rapid Response Revival alerted the TGA twice – in 2019 and 2021 – that the CellAED manufacturer was deceiving Australians and potential investors.

Advertisement

“This company continues to raise funds through deceptive means – providing false information about their product and company’s capabilities, readiness to manufacture, timelines and actual orders and regulatory approvals,” said the 2021 complaint, obtained by this masthead. The senior executive, who wanted to remain anonymous for legal reasons, said he never received a response from the regulator. The man, who has extensive experience working for some of the world’s largest medical device manufacturers, was recruited to Rapid Response Revival by an executive search firm. But he said that within two days he realised something wasn’t right. “It seemed like a lot of smoke and mirrors,” he recalled of his short stint at the company in 2019. “I could see this device had the potential to cause real harm. A patient experiencing cardiac arrest needs a working AED that has gone through rigorous regulatory processes. I knew that without proper standards, this product was going to cost someone their life.” CellAED is a case study for many of the problems with Australia’s regulation of medical devices.

Advertisement

With no clinical evidence to prove it could save lives, the device bypassed Australian scrutiny by obtaining approval from a private German device evaluator. This for-profit company eventually approved the device – allowing it to be automatically approved for sale in Australia in September 2021. More than 23,000 units have been sold or donated, including to ambulance services in Victoria and Canberra. When the whistleblower asked for clinical evidence supporting the device, he claims founder Donovan Casey showed him a video of a pig being shocked by a CellAED. “When they discharged the energy during the test, the pig jumped off the table,” he said. “It absolutely didn’t restart the pig’s heart, all it did was show it delivered energy.” He said the company originally tried to obtain TGA registration but was told by the watchdog in a pre-application discussion that they needed “human data”.

Advertisement

The whistleblower said after this discussion, the company flipped strategy and decided to seek registration overseas. His account is backed up by a leaked company photograph of scrawlings on a whiteboard which read: “Our current clinical evaluation report would not be sufficient for the TGA to approve the device”. Loading The whistleblower described CellAED as a “carbon copy of Theranos” – a reference to the fraudulent health start-up founded by American Elizabeth Holmes, which spurred a popular podcast and television miniseries. A 2019 clinical evaluation report, submitted to the private German company that eventually approved the CellAED for sale, highlights the lack of evidence supporting the device. Medical devices can be approved on the back of clinical trials showing they are safe and effective. Alternatively, manufacturers can use ‘equivalence’: claiming their device is the same as an already-approved device. The defibrillator generates just 85 joules, well below the 200 joules recommended by Australian defibrillation guidelines.

Advertisement

The 2019 evaluation report claimed the CellAED was equivalent to the FRED Easyport, which delivers shocks with 150 joules of energy. The only actual data presented was from tests on two female pigs. The test was run while the pigs’ hearts were beating normally; it confirmed the device could electrocute a pig, but did not show it could restart their heart. “To date, no human clinical studies have been performed,” the report noted. The report presented a 2008 Bulgarian study as further evidence the device worked. But that study was also conducted using much higher energy levels than the CellAED could deliver. This masthead provided the 2019 report to Australian Resuscitation Council deputy chair Michael Parr to review. Based on the report, “a reviewer cannot tell if the device actually works”, he said. “The device did not demonstrate efficacy or true equivalence.”

title: Their Byron neighbours live in $2m homes. These villagers are being evicted
text:

PoliticsNSWPlanning Their Byron neighbours live in $2m homes. These villagers are being evicted Amber Schultz August 4, 2026 — 11:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The anxiety is palpable at the Northern Rivers temporary pod villages as eviction day looms. The villages consist of dozens of demountables set up on council land, including a village on Tweed Street in Brunswick Heads, following the devastating 2022 floods. They sit alongside a booming real estate market where three-bedroom homes sell for more than $2 million. Only six temporary pod villages remain, following the decommissioning of five others last year. Residents not on a social housing waitlist were told to vacate last week, while the remaining 167 households have until September, ahead of full decommissioning in December. But in a region with rental vacancies of 0.5 per cent, locals say there’s nowhere to go.

Advertisement

Residents told this masthead they’ve been offered unofficial cash-in-hand rentals that render them ineligible for additional financial support. Others rent discounted Airbnbs only to be displaced when peak-season bookings arrive. One elderly resident said she was advised to get rid of her pets to secure accommodation, with the stress making her feel like she was going to have a heart attack. Some are still paying mortgages for unlivable properties as they await resilience funding to rebuild. Suebee has lost count of the number of rentals she’s applied for. She said some won’t accept pets or kids. Natalie Grono There’s been a 41 per cent increase in the number of rough sleepers people counted in Lismore since 2020, according to Homes NSW statewide street count. Suebee* and her 15-year-old son have moved multiple times since their Mullumbimby rental was flooded in 2022. After bouncing between short-term rentals and staying with friends, they moved into the Brunswick Heads pod village in 2023.

Advertisement

“I’ve lost track of the number of times we’ve had to move, find accommodation and apply for rentals,” she said. Stable accommodation enabled Suebee, who lives with chronic fatigue and PTSD following the 2017 floods, to secure stable work. Staying in the region has also allowed her son to remain at the same high school, where she said support has been “incredible”. The Lismore temporary housing village will also be decommissioned in December. Brook Mitchell “With housing security you can consistently show up for employment and for your community versus when you’re floundering in survival mode,” she said. Suebee contributes 30 per cent of her income to Homes NSW, which manages the villages, and must submit proof of regular rental applications. To meet this quota, she applies for properties outside her budget, resulting in rejections. “It’s demoralising,” she said.

Advertisement

“For rental agencies, we’re at the bottom of the list compared to two-income households.” Jasmine** moved into the village with her 10-year-old daughter in November 2025 after their rental burned down in an electrical fire. She was told to vacate by July 29, so she secured a rental, but it fell through when the landlord decided to sell. ‘I just thought, I cannot be homeless and lose a parent at the same time.’ Jasmine, who lives in the village with her daughter, 10 “I completely broke down; the eviction date was nine days away,” she said. Adding to her stress, her critically ill mother was also taken to hospital. “I just thought, I cannot be homeless and lose a parent at the same time. I was sick; all the stress of uncertainty caught up with me,” she said.

Advertisement

Her extension came through less than 24 hours before her eviction date, and she now has until September 30 to find somewhere else. Judy Corner is 84 and moved into the village in February after years of short-term or insecure housing. Most of her belongings are in storage. Judy Corner, 84, said she worries about the other residents’ mental health due to the constant threat of eviction. Natalie Grono She’s on a priority social housing list but, given the looming eviction date, has been calling Homes NSW for months to be bumped up to the highest priority list. The ombudsman is now assisting. “The anxiety has been palpable, you can feel it in the air,” she said.

Advertisement

“At my age, I can’t sleep in a car. I want quality of life.” She said she’s been offered an aged care placement, but isn’t ready to give up her independence. Related Article Exclusive

Tragedy A mother had been living in a tent for months. Then she went into labour Homes NSW said there have been 249 social and affordable homes made available since 2023, with another 154 expected by June 2027. A spokesperson said relocations from the villages were being staggered to ensure residents can receive “the maximum amount of support in securing other housing options”. “Supporting residents to transition to appropriate long-term accommodation remains the priority,” the spokesperson said. The spokesperson said no one had been left homeless following the earlier closure of pod villages, but would not confirm how long they monitored residents.

Advertisement

The pods have been flagged for use to support affordable, social, transitional, crisis or key worker housing, with specific uses expected to be finalised by the end of the year. Related Article Exclusive

Crime Belinda thought she had bought her dream Byron home. It soon turned into a nightmare Byron Council Shire Mayor Sarah Ndiaye said unlike neighbouring councils, no new social or public homes have been delivered in the shire. “Pushing people out of the pods before there is anywhere for them to actually go feels cruel and premature,” she said. “For many in the time since the floods, those things are the only stability some people have had.”

She’s advocating for the villages to remain, with the option for those who don’t qualify for social housing are charged market rent. Related Article Exclusive

Domestic violence Inside Sydney’s neonatal refuge where staff carry panic buttons Founder of housing advocacy group House You, Chels Hood Withey, who has been assisting residents in their social housing applications, said the villages were already functioning as community housing and should continue to do so. “Every time the funding runs out, the residents get given letters and live in complete fear,” she said. “We know so many who are homeless, and it breaks your heart.”

title: ‘Shock and hurt’: The religious meeting that left Sydney private school old girls fuming
text:
Advertisement

NationalNSWEducation ‘Shock and hurt’: The religious meeting that left Sydney private school old girls fuming Christopher Harris August 4, 2026 — 11:38am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The head of one of Sydney’s high-fee girls’ schools has acknowledged the “shock and hurt” triggered by a vote of the Presbyterian Church’s NSW general assembly held on its campus to exclude women from some future leadership roles within the religion. Members of the church’s general assembly met last month at PLC Sydney’s Audrey Keown Theatre and voted in a two-thirds majority to restrict women from becoming elders – mature Christian leaders within the church who are chosen by a congregation. PLC Sydney is associated with and reports to the Presbyterian Church. Steven Siewert It prompted numerous ex-students to contact the school to complain, including former school captain Ruth Mueller who wrote that she found the decision “deeply troubling”. “The decision sends a message that no matter how faithful, capable, experienced, or called a woman may be, there remains a level of leadership she cannot attain simply because she is a woman,” she wrote.

Advertisement

Dr Rosie Shorter, who graduated from the school in 2000, wrote a letter to school principal Paul Burgis – signed by almost 100 ex-students – asking him to respond to the vote to exclude women. Related Article HSC When things go wrong inside Sydney’s most expensive schools “The reason I wrote to the school was because I felt there was actually a safety issue in the vote,” she said. “Obviously, the school didn’t make the decision – the general assembly did – but making the decision to reverse the opportunity for women to be elders, it is setting up a form of gender inequality.” In the face of the anger of the ex-students, Burgis wrote to the school community last Wednesday.

Advertisement

“I am an employee of the College and external to church decisions, but I do know of the College Council’s supreme commitment to the education of young women and girls,” he said. He listed numerous high-profile ex-students who have gone on to be leaders across science, medicine, politics, sport and the arts, including University of Sydney pro vice-chancellor Katherine Belov, former Supreme Court justice Carolyn Simpson and former Australian senator Kerry Nettle. That letter infuriated several former students even further. “What disappointed me most was not only the decision itself, but the absence of empathy in your response,” wrote Susie Lawson, who graduated in 1989, in a subsequent letter to Burgis.

Advertisement

“Perhaps what saddens me most is imagining the message this sends to today’s students. We encourage our girls to believe they can become judges, surgeons, scientists, CEOs or prime ministers, yet they now see that within the governing church of their own school there remain leadership positions unavailable to them simply because they are women.” Another former student, Dr Sandra O’Toole, also responded to the principal to say the school’s history of producing outstanding women should not be used to “soften the impact” of the decision that ultimately limits women’s authority. “The school cannot take pride in the achievements of its alumnae while remaining too cautious about a decision that diminishes women’s leadership within the church that governs it,” she said. “I would have hoped to see the school denounce the implication that women are unsuitable for particular forms of leadership, rather than seek to reassure the community while appearing to accommodate or defend the decision.” PLC Sydney principal Dr Paul Burgis

Advertisement

Dr Burgis wrote a further letter to the school community on Friday, noting the volume of emails and messages expressing dissatisfaction with the decision. “It is fair to say that there were three common elements in the feedback: an overwhelming sense of shock and hurt that this overture was supported by the Church, that it occurred on our school grounds, and that my initial communication didn’t fully cover the issue,” he wrote. He said he had very “very strong feelings” about the issue and would express them to the college council, the church at the highest levels, and via his local presbytery. Women have been allowed to serve as elders in the church in NSW since the 1960s, unlike in the Queensland and Victorian sections of the church.

Advertisement

Under the church’s barrier act, the “overture” voted on last month would then be sent to all regional presbyteries (church governing bodies) for approval, which Burgis said was consultative and expected to take around 12 months. If the majority approve it, the overture returns to a future general assembly for final ratification before becoming church practice. “Some ex-students have been asking for me to voice my opinion clearly in the media. It is very important to recognise that the church has a wide-ranging internal consultative process that has not yet begun,” Burgis said. In response to questions from Herald, Burgis said he’d been assured it would have no impact on school governance, operations, teachings, or culture. “We will continue uncompromised in our 140 years of tradition regardless of the outcome of the next 12 months of Church-led consultation on this matter before any decision is made on whether the proposed change becomes Church law.”

title: ‘You’re terrible, Muriel’ made Gabby a minor celebrity. Her new career is making her happy
text:
Gabby Millgate ate at the Balmain Bowling Club with her family when she was in high school.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Muriel’s Wedding came out in 1994, I was in my first year of a communications degree in Bathurst, majoring in journalism – and Thursday nights at the uni bar. Gabby Millgate, who played Muriel’s sister, was a theatre media major in the same course. A straw poll of younger Australians – based on a handful of my 20-something colleagues – suggests that even those who have never seen Muriel’s Wedding know Millgate’s immortal line “you’re terrible, Muriel”. At the peak of the movie’s success, international celebrities including Madonna and Will Ferrell said the line on television, trying their best to mimic Millgate’s Aussie drawl and exact tone of horrified delight. Millgate uttered the line three times in the movie as Joanie Heslop, and has since repeated it hundreds of times as herself. At one point, she anonymously called in to a radio contest for who could say the line the best – and lost. In the 2000s she became friends with Kyle Sandilands, and he often called her from various nightclubs at 3am with different companions, begging “say the line, say the line”. (His agent confirms this is true.) When Millgate repeats the line now, she likes to personalise it. “You’re terrible, Caitlin,” she says to demonstrate, when we meet up for lunch 30 years after we last saw each other.

Advertisement

“I like seeing people light up because the movie means so much to them,” Millgate says. “I know it happens to me when I meet people who are culturally important in my life – like when I met Molly Meldrum, I was like, ‘oh, my God, if he’s real, the Road Runner is real’, and my mother had a meltdown.” Gabby Millgate sits down over lunch at Balmain Bowling Club. Renee Nowytarger We meet at the Balmain Bowling Club in Sydney’s inner west where Millgate spent many happy evenings with her family when she was a teenager. She orders the same meal she always ate on nights at the bowlo – a bowl of steamed green vegetables and a bowl of chips. I have a Caesar salad and convince her to share a starter of prawn dumplings. Steamed greens, chips and Caesar salad at Balmain Bowling Club. Renee Nowytarger A starter of prawn dumplings at Balmain Bowling Club. Renee Nowytarger As if to prove the only constant in life is change, Millgate texts me just as I put the finishing touches on this article to say that her parents have sold the family home in Balmain and moved to Canberra to be near their daughters and grandchildren. I text back that the bowlo – the oldest in Sydney – has closed as well. “Nooo!” she says. “The universe is crumbling behind me – no going back.” Millgate moved from Canberra with her family in senior high school when her stepfather became chief censor in the Office of Film and Literature Classification – a job that meant he later saw Muriel’s Wedding before anyone else, though he had to recuse himself from the rating decision.

Advertisement

After finishing school at St Scholastica’s in Glebe in inner-city Sydney, Millgate fell in love with theatre sports before getting her big break in Muriel’s Wedding in her early 20s, in what she describes as her “Alice in Wonderland moment”. Millgate went to university as a mature-age student, then landed a gig on the comedy show Full Frontal. After that came a bit part in the sequel to Babe and a role on Celebrity Big Brother where she met Sandilands. He helped her get a job in commercial breakfast radio in Brisbane, but she soon realised it wasn’t for her. “It was like working on the Death Star,” she says. Millgate came back to Sydney, popping up as a regular caller on the Kyle and Jackie O Show playing a character called Debbie who was perpetually angry at the hosts. Millgate as Joanie Heslop. Robert McFarlane She then moved to the Pilbara, returning to radio as an ABC host, and later working as an educational officer at a prison. For the radio job, she travelled around the region doing stories and met a listener in Port Hedland who lived off grid with solar power, tank water, cows, chickens and vegetable gardens. “I drove out to see him, and him and I went collecting cow manure together,” she says. “We struck up an unlikely friendship, as much as you can with someone who lives two hours away.” This experience later proved relevant in Millgate’s reinvention story. She was back in Sydney when Julia Gillard became prime minister, and decided to try her hand as a Gillard impersonator. That lasted a few years, until Gillard was deposed. At that point, Millgate gave up trying to make a living in show business. She realised that Muriel’s Wedding had not been a launchpad for bigger and better things, but rather the pinnacle.

Advertisement

In many ways, Millgate’s acting career was a story of struggling to find a place amid contracting opportunities. Partly, she reflects, this was a structural shift because a show like Full Frontal that curated culture was no longer viable in Australia in an era where every individual curated their own culture. Partly it was because her early success had skewed her expectations. “Because it had been such a random event to get Muriel’s in the first place, I thought that was my destiny, and that life would just keep handing me big destiny moments like that,” Millgate says. “Whereas the reality is, for everybody not blessed by random events, that you need to start at the bottom and work your way up. “I was helicoptered to the top of the mountain that a lot of people struggle and strive to climb. Coming down from there, I didn’t even know the landscape, which had mental health issues that came along with it, and [a sense of] losing purpose, and all of that sort of thing. I felt like I had the potential to be a pot of gold, but I was being used as a doorstop.” Pic shows Julia Spillard aka Gabby Millgate. Michel O'Sullivan At the age of 42, Millgate decided to retrain as an early childhood educator. As we discuss it over lunch, she doesn’t miss the opportunity to joke about 42 being the meaning of life per Douglas Adams’ Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy. Millgate says she is much happier than she was as a performer because she feels useful with her skills and abilities serving families and children. She has a sense of a natural give and take, whereas comedy and media was all “give, give, give”. “It was hard, but I also actually trust in the process of giving up,” Millgate says. “I know in our society, we’re supposed to try our best all the time, but sometimes you need renewal by accepting the world you’ve created has come to a finale, but you’re still alive in the world.”

Advertisement

Millgate had never even changed a nappy when she got her first early childhood teaching job in a room full of two-year-olds in a centre in Balmain. “By the end of the year, I could recognise who needed changing just by the distinct aroma,” she says. The children were kept indoors most of the day in a room set up to replicate the outdoors, with pot plants and a sandpit and a bike track. They were meant to visit a nearby park at least once a day, but with steep stairs and staff shortages as obstacles, it did not always happen. She later moved back to Canberra to be closer to her sister and her niece and nephew, and started working at a centre that had outdoor space. It was just a bare backyard with a small plastic slide and a sandpit, but Millgate worked with the children to create a lush garden with bean tunnels, nasturtiums and snow peas. “I’ve seen the difference it makes in children’s wellbeing, and how just being able to go outside and see a chicken or be barefoot on the grass can really help them self-regulate,” Millgate says. “They like digging in the ground and finding worms. Finding an egg is so exciting for them.” Gabby Millgate says it was hard to give up on show business, but it’s the best decision she’s ever made. Renee Nowytarger They built a dry riverbed because one day they had the tap on and the children started asking questions about why the water flowed in a certain direction. That meant the children were learning what Millgate calls “ecological literacy skills” by following their own interests and having conversations. “Regular literacy is learning the letters so that we can understand language,” she explains. “Ecological literacy, instead of ABCD, we’ve got dirt, mud, rock, sticks, seeds, plants, beans, worms, bugs, logs, chickens, all of those things.”

title: ‘Turn up’: Demand on Pauline after media ban
text:
A cabinet minister has called on One Nation leader Pauline Hanson to "be accountable" after she barred several media outlets from attending a press conference.

Reporters from the ABC, The Age and The Guardian were denied entry to Senator Hanson's press conference in Melbourne on Monday where she announced candidates for the upcoming Victorian election.

Asked by other reporters why the outlets were not let in, Senator Hanson said: "I'm sorry that democracy doesn't happen on the ABC at all. And I'm sick of it, it's not fair and just in their reporting."

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Employment and Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth said on Tuesday that politicians "have to turn up and answer questions".

Employment and Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth says politicians 'have to turn up and answer questions'. Picture: Nine/Today

"By saying you've got nothing to hide. I don't know why she would want to, well, bar ABC The Age, The Guardian," she told Nine's Today.

Ms Rishworth said that Senator Hanson had been "caught out a few times" by the media, referencing her stance towards paid parental leave, but insisted all media outlets should be allowed to report on her views.

"I'm not sure who was left at her press conference, but, quite frankly, you need to be accountable," she said.

"You need to turn up. Sometimes the questions are uncomfortable."

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Speaking to radio later, Senator Hanson said the media ban "won't be forever and a day" and insisted the outlets would be allowed back when they "give us a fair go".

"I did it in 1996 for nine months with the ABC and finally they started doing fair reporting," she said.

"It won't be forever and a day but it's like putting out a message – give us a fair go."

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson says she does not 'answer to media'. Picture: NewsWire / Martin Ollman

Senator Hanson previously declared she does not "answer to the media" and would continue to dodge the ABC and other outlets in her address to the National Press Club in June.

"The ABC has proven itself been completely in denial about its profoundly transparent political bias and the activists in its ranks … the arrogance is stunning in its scope," she said at the time.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"It is partly for this reason I have, at times, refused ABC interviews.

"I will continue to do so because, as media outlets go, the ABC is very low on my list of priorities and their bias against One Nation and me is obvious."

In her comments on Tuesday, Ms Rishworth said all political parties should strive for transparency.

"The (Australian Electoral Commission) has very clear rules and they have become more transparent," she said.

"Every political party should do so."

title: 'A robe and nothing else': Alan Jones' alleged order
text:
Alan Jones wanted "easy access" to a young athlete's naked body when he ordered him to dress only in a robe before indecently assaulting him, according to his alleged victim.

The 85-year-old veteran broadcaster is facing the first week of a months-long Local Court hearing after he pleaded not guilty to 22 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching without consent.

The man told the court Jones grabbed his genitals while he was driving to the NSW Southern Highlands and squeezed painfully tight, causing him to veer off the road.
